The early K-type star K2-138, hosting six planets, particularly five proposed to be in a prolonged chain of 3:2 mean motion resonances, necessitates the analysis of its planets' potential resonant behavior. By using existing parameters in N-body simulations, our analysis confirms that nearly all simulations (99.2%) produce a chain of 3:2 resonances; however, fewer (11%) demonstrate a five-planet resonance chain. We successfully employ resonances to confine the orbital periods and masses of the planets. We examine the likelihood of this system forming in situ and through disk migration, as well as explore the potential planetary compositions using a computational planet structure model. Our results suggest that planets around the ring of resonances have lower heavy element masses compared to those outside the resonance. The constraints on planetary properties and masses are presented. The data and simulations are available for download at http://www.astro.upf.edu/users/dragons/ K2-138.html. We explore the potential observational signatures of the planets inside the resonance chain, including tidal interactions and possible future transit configurations. The planets in the resonance chain have increased tidal heating activity due to resonant catastles within the simulation constraints, as well as augmented ring systems. The increased tidal heating is likely to shorten the lifetime of the ring system; however, low initial ring widths may lead to the destruction of the ring within a relatively short astronomical time unit for planets within the resonance chain near the ring's inner edge. We also observe that the planets in the resonance chain have potential transits that could be identified with the Juan Carlos I telescope, as well as larger telescopes such as Haute Provence and LOFAR, which could enhance our understanding of the planets' properties and their formation mechanisms. Using advanced computer simulations, researchers studied the molecular structure of water in hexagonal ice (Ih) and low-density amorphous ice (LDA) at low temperatures under high pressure conditions. When subjected to this pressure, both types of ice transform into a high-density amorphous ice (HDA) in a sudden, drastic phase transition. An innovative measure, based on the arrangement of oxygen atoms in the ice structure, allowed the researchers to confirm that LDA and HDA do not contain separate, distinct ice domains. While the resulting HDA structure still exhibits certain characteristics of both its components, it is predominantly similar to Ih ice in terms of its arrangement. Interestingly, this finding shows that a sudden, drastic phase transition can occur without requiring a high density of defects in the transformed material. It is further supported by a finding that, even at very high pressures, both LDA and HDA exhibit similar excess entropy, a key indicator of their structural similarity. Therefore, this research suggests that their high-pressure transformation from LDA to HDA may involve a gradual transition via an disordered state with a structure similar to Ih ice. It is further suggested that this transition could be blocked if LDA and HDA are composed of mixtures with distinct ice structures. (Figure presented here is for promotional purposes only.)

While we successfully measure wave properties, the underlying physics driving these phenomena often remains unclear. Interactions between ultralow frequency (ULF) waves and particles are particularly important in shaping magnetospheric plasma, affecting the trajectory of particles and transferring energy. Although we have comprehensive wave measurements, magnetic field data alone is insufficient to determine the full three-dimensional structure of these waves on small scales. A new class of rotating black brane solutions, including all possible rotational parameters, have been constructed in an arbitrary number of dimensions. These rotating black branes are flat in topology at their horizons, yet due to the influence of the dilaton field, they do not conform to either flat or (anti)-de Sitter asymptotic behaviors. We've analyzed the physical properties of these rotating black branes by applying a counterterm method. In this method, we've determined the mass and angular momentum for these rotating black branes in dimensions of arbitrary size. The counterterm approach has allowed us to establish the first law of thermodynamics for these rotating black branes and to verify the holographic system's consistency by showing that its free energy is equal to the free energy determined by thermodynamics. The research also indicates that these rotating black branes undergo a first-order phase transition. Furthermore, the thermal stability of these rotating black brines has been investigated by analyzing the eigenvalues of the relevant Hessian matrices, which has led to the finding that these solutions are thermally unstable. The effect of the coupling constant on thermodynamic parameters has been studied in detail. In the era of artificial intelligence, computational advancements in text analysis are crucial. Multiple systems have been created to process text across various languages. We introduce a novel, knowledge-based text analysis framework that aims to represent text similar to how we store it - as memories. We provide a detailed explanation of each module and support our approach with experimental results from three key projects: a knowledge-based thesaurus for Arabic, a semantic search engine for Arabic and English, and an automatic text summarizer for Arabic. Our results demonstrate the superiority of our framework over traditional machine learning methods in terms of performance metrics and cost comparisons with baseline systems. We generated theoretical forecasts for the cm-wavelength free-free emission produced by two distinct disk models, tailored to the TW Hydrae young stellar object, and analyzed how photoevaporation affects this phenomenon. According to our analysis, the high-energy photons from the star in this system can drive disk photoevaporation and create a transition zone between the inner disk regions and the wind zone. By combining observed dust emission and the photoevaporation model, we estimated the disk's vertical pressure and found that the radio emission from the TW Hydrae system could be entirely produced by the Kelvin-Helmholtz mechanism if the disk's mass is less than 10% of what it would be in the absence of photoevaporation. Conversely, a combination of MHD disk wind and photoevaporation models can also explain the observed radio flux with minimal disk mass loss, which would be on the order of millimeters per second. Radio Astronomers may be able to detect variations in the "jet-like" outflows from the TW Hydrae system with the assistance of the Next Generation Very Large Array, allowing for the validation of the MHD disk wind model through the detection of variations in the ejection rate. Conversely, if no variations are detected, it could indicate that the observed "jet-like" structure is primarily the result of the disk photoevaporation model. Ultimately, these predictions demonstrate the potential for the Next Generation Very Large Array to serve as an effective tool for the experimental testing of theoretical astrophysical models, particularly those relating to the observed "disk winds" in the TW Hydrae system. We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with rotational movement influenced by both elasticity and friction. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the spectrum's asymptotic distribution and structure evolve. It demonstrates that specific eigenvector characteristics form a complete and orthonormal basis. Consequently, we derive the exponential stability of the associated semigroup directly. Notably, we find that under these connectivity conditions, stability is guaranteed even in the absence of elasticity along the edges. This outcome contrasts with previous findings, highlighting the significance of rotational fixity and interior node degrees in graph stability. Additionally, we illustrate how these connectivity conditions intersect with neutrally stable points, prompting further exploration into linearized and semilinear stability analyses. The development of pattern extraction algorithms helps gain valuable insights into ever-growing datasets by translating recurring data features into simplified representations. However, as dataset volumes and complexities increase, the number of discovered patterns grows exponentially, overwhelming analysts with an extensive result space. Most existing algorithms and visualization methods struggle to answer key overview questions, hindering the understanding of pattern distributions, qualities, and interconnections. To tackle this issue, we propose a visual analytics pipeline that automatically facilitates the exploration of region-based patterns in large datasets, especially those of geospatial nature. Our approach aims to support multi-scale reasoning by leveraging visualizations at various levels, including sub-regions, regions, and the entire dataset, as well as integrating an interactive map to discover related spatial entities and patterns across multiple scales. To ensure the efficiency of our approach, we capitalize on open geospatial data sources and web mapping technologies, augmenting the customization of visual representations to address different analysis priorities. A crucial challenge in the study of rarefied gas dynamics lies in determining the steady-state solution of the Boltzmann equation efficiently. The conventional iteration method often achieves rapid convergence at low Knudsen numbers, yet it is hindered by prolonged and error-prone computations at higher numbers. To address this limitation, this paper suggests an initial and iterative procedure, known as the iteration towards equilibrium (ITE), to obtain steady-state solutions of the Boltzmann equation. By leveraging scaling arguments, the ITE method enables the creation of straightforward and computationally effective macroscopic corrections. Furthermore, it ensures that the iteratively obtained solutions from the microscopic level conform to the requirements of valid rarefied gas flow models, thereby preventing unphysical phenomena. To validate and demonstrate the efficacy of the ITE method, it is applied to various exemplary cases, including a straightforward scenario involving two dissimilar solid boundaries and a more complex example featuring periodic patterns of thin dissimilar microstructures. The results derived using the ITE method are then compared with those obtained through iterations alone, while the method's computational efficacy is further substantiated by scaling analyses and actual computations. Lastly, to expand the scope and versatility of the ITE method, it is also used to re-examine the solution of a specific variant of the inhomogeneous two-temperature Maxwellian molecule model, where the ITE method's efficiency and robustness serve as a strong indicator of its potential for broad applications in the field of rarefied gas dynamics. The paper concludes by discussing the various potential avenues of extension and applications for the ITE method and the Boltzmann equation in particular. Furthermore, it is also used to develop a theoretical explanation for the observed regularities in the solutions obtained in the inhomogeneous two-temperature Maxwellian molecule model. The creation of such theoretical underpinnings and rational modifications of the ITE method could further establish its trustworthiness and credibility in the study of rarefied gas dynamics. The primary portion continues to travel at light speed, preserving energy, while the secondary portion is absorbed by the plasma, producing a substantial increase in temperature. The condition necessary for the formation of a steepening, extremely powerful laser beam in a vacuum has also been identified, which corresponds to a critical intensity of 3.26 x 10^14 cm^-2. The separation of the laser beam into two portions is accompanied by the creation of a substantial, transient electric field between them, which can reach a strength of 4.67 x 10^11 V/m at a distance of one micron, capable of providing full electron depletion over a short period of time, thereby offering a novel means of introducing electrons into a pre-existing plasma in a highly controlled and rapid manner. Furthermore, we have determined the condition under which the separation of the laser beam results in the acceleration of electrons, which can reach a maximum energy of 7.94 x 10 GW centimeters. This study investigates the capabilities of color-plus-mono dual-camera systems, where the color sensor often features a smaller active area than the mono sensor, posing a further challenge. To fully leverage the data from both sensors, we need to address two key alignment issues: first, synchronizing the data from the color and mono sensors, which is often difficult due to their differing frame rates; and second, aligning the image coordinates across the two sensors, which is complicated by their varying active areas. Through extensive experiments, we found that simply averaging the color and mono values leads to significant color distortion, especially under harsh lighting conditions. To address these challenges, we developed a novel image registration technique that synchronizes the data from the two sensors, based on the motion between frames. We also introduced a novel image warping technique that accurately aligns the image coordinates across the two sensors, using a deep neural network that learns a weighted average of the corresponding points across the two sensors. To optimize the performance of our proposed methods, we employed a dual-loss training approach, consisting of a adversarial loss and a mean squared error loss. Two related variations of the well-known knapsack problem are the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem. Each involves selecting items from a set to maximize an objective while adhering to a budget limit and a set of nonnegative item values and quantities. We propose a new search-based algorithm, called Budgeted Set-Union Coverage (BSUC), to solve these problems efficiently. We introduce two variants of the BSUC algorithm: one optimized for the SUKP and another for the BMCP. The BSUC approach iteratively selects items up to the budget, taking into account quality, a candidate solution's cost, and the number of uncovered elements. We prove the algorithm's effectiveness and efficiency through various theoretical guarantees. Experimental results show the BSUC algorithm outperforms existing solutions by up to 1000 times in runtime. Notably, the BSUC algorithm serves as a starting point for a new heuristic method, called the SUKP Tabu Search, which achieves superior results compared to the state-of-the-art SUKP heuristic recently proposed by Chen et al. We also demonstrate the generalizability of the BSUC algorithm through its successful application in solving the BMCP. This inspiring real-world BMCP instance originally proposed by Bringmann et al. involves selecting the cheapest set of research papers to maximize citations and remains unsolved for almost a decade. Our new BMCP solver, the BSUC algorithm, successfully finds a solution with 100% coverage and a minimal cost, thus answering the long-standing open question and showcasing the BSUC algorithm's promise. The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key Hilbert space unitary 
isomorphisms that explain the dual nature of waves and particles and the 
interplay between configuration space and phase space. This study generalizes 
those concepts to functions that use Clifford algebra. It defines unitary 
isomorphisms among spaces consisting of square-integrable Clifford algebra-valued 
functions on n-dimensional space, monogenic square-integrable functions on n+1 
dimensional space, and linear functionals on symmetric tensor elements in n 
dimensional space, each space weighted by a respective Gaussian measure. The 
generalized theory provides a framework for doing quantum mechanics over a field 
that is not the complex numbers, allowing the exploration of parity-nonconserving 
quantum field theories. Although this study focuses on Clifford algebra-valued 
functions, it can be applied to similar problems in higher dimensions. Our work 
makes use of Taylor isomorphism, the reversion operator, and Gabor-like 
representations of Clifford algebra generators. It describes a representation of 
the coordinate and momentum operators as left- and right-multiplications in a 
specific Hilbert space. This study identifies key operator identities that provide 
a link between different representation spaces and develops a coherent operator 
version of the Segal-Bargmann theory. Our work also makes use of Zimmert's theorem 
and the Fenchel-And\^o mean-value inequality to establish positivity results in 
Clifford algebra. It maintains the spirit of simplicity that defines the 
original Segal-Bargmann theory. This study is a shortened, revised, and 
revised version of the authors' earlier work in 2019. It is part of the 
author's doctoral thesis. The presentation has been adjusted for better 
understandability.

As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as an intermediary between complicated mathematical formulas and applicable predictions through random sampling. Traditional techniques for generating samples from Gaussian process posterior calculations consider samples as separate draws from the distribution of process values at fixed points. This focus on distribution characteristics leads to strategies that increase exponentially with the desired dimensionality. This becomes impractical for large dimensions, prompting us to consider a new line of thinking, where Gaussian conditionals are viewed in the context of individual random variables. This alternative interpretation, which involves conditionals as random variables, allows us to derive and evaluate approximation techniques that support efficient Gaussian process posterior sampling. By examining the underpinning principles, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in approximating Gaussian processes and assess their practical value in applied settings like optimization and reinforcement learning. The issue of low accuracy in predicting far-off frames has been addressed by enhancing the basic PL model, but another problem of inconsistent prediction error remains, where closer predictions tend to have lower errors than farther ones. We tested our approach, named MoDeRNN, on the benchmark dataset SUMO and compared it to well-known spatiotemporal change detection datasets and state-of-the-art methods. Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in numerous applications, but their applicability is restricted by the costly and time-consuming process of manual maintenance. Current research has sought to automatically enhance taxonomies by learning concept representations in Euclidean space. However, the natural geometric structure of taxonomies aligns better with hyperbolic properties, making this space more suitable for representation. We propose HyperExpan, an algorithm that preserves the hierarchical structure of a taxonomy within a more expressive hyperbolic embedding space. It employs graph neural networks to capture relationships and characterizes profile information of concepts for accurate prediction during training. HyperExpan surpasses the performance of baseline models that utilize Euclidean space representation learning and achieves state-of-the-art results in taxonomy expansion benchmarks. Additionally, we develop and present a new benchmark, called AppEx, that targets the under-explored area of mobile app categorization in hyperbolic space. The implementation of HyperExpan can be found on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/kaitoasakura/ HyperExpan. The taxonomy datasets and experiments have been made publicly available for replication at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7372466. 

The key contributions of this research are threefold:
- We make the first state-of-the-art hyperbolic taxonomy embedding model for classification and knowledge base completion tasks.
- We introduce a new and challenging benchmark, titled AppEx, for modeling large-scale hierarchical taxonomies in hyperbolic space.
- We compare the performance of hyperbolic and traditional embedding approaches, and highlight the expressiveness and geometric properties of hyperbolic space in capturing hierarchical structures. Moreover, we adapt a neural network to learn concept representations in hyperbolic space, and show its strong generalization on the AppEx through an analysis of its eigenvalue distribution. The research also identifies the limitations of hyperbolic space embedding models, such as the difficulty in training due to complex edge-weight distributions, and the requirement of additional supervision for effective training. Finally, we suggest the need for more research on hyperbolic embedding models for a range of practical tasks. The research further reveals the advantages of hyperbolic space over Euclidean space in modeling taxonomy hierarchies, and the potential of hyperbolic embedding models to achieve state-of-the-art results on the AppEx benchmark through graph neural network-based learning. In real-world manufacturing settings, unexpected events inevitably cause task delays, further complicating scheduling tasks. Uncertainty regarding such events and their potential durations is often hard to predict, leading to combinatorial complications in scheduling algorithms. In many cases, tasks with uncertain completion times are approximated by assigning either optimistic or pessimistic projected due dates. This study explores a novel approach to integrate uncertainty into scheduling algorithms by modeling a task's range of possible completion times between an earliest and latest finish time. This flexible framework allows for automatic adjustments by sliding both completion times based on the current progress made so far towards meeting the scheduled latest finish times. In Level Due Date Scheduling algorithms, reducing slack on the optimistic side requires increasing the latest finish time, while reducing slack on the pessimistic side involves advancing the earliest finish time. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization. It is found that sources with flat spectra tend to have higher polarization. These findings are consistent with the presence of a transition size between strongly and weakly depolarized radio sources. Moreover, the results indicate radio sources larger than ~8'" generally exhibit low polarization. These conditions will influence the performance of radio interferometers, particularly the Planck-Lensing program, which relies on radio sources to observe the cosmic microwave background. Based on these conditions, the Planck Low Frequency Instrument may fail to detect the gravitational lensing effect for certain source size bins below ~8'" or specific polarization ranges. Future radio surveys with high signal-to-noise ratio and low uncertainty in source position will allow for stacking analysis to estimate polarization properties more effectively. It is expected that future large-scale radio surveys may achieve such conditions, yielding better estimates of gravitational lensing in the cosmic microwave background. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model based on Markov processes, but with the critical difference of having some components hidden from observation. HMMs are used extensively in fields like speech recognition and are essential tools for analyzing Markov processes, especially when there's limited data available. HMMs present several issues for an abstract analysis: they can't be properly represented as total relations, and their lack of compositionality in an epimorphic sense means they can't be effectively generalized to other types of models. The concept of information flow is also inherently tricky, as it's difficult to determine what's being discussed. To address this, an earlier paper proposed the use of a specific monad called the stochastic monad, which seems to handle HMMs in a clean and effective manner, but only for finite models. To address the issue of dealing with infinite model states, this paper proposes a more general version of the stochastic monad, which can also handle used in an analogous way to describe Markov processes, especially when dealing with partial observations and the likelihood of uncertainty. The paper also explains how a type called a partial commutative monoid describes HMMs and other types of Markov models, providing a fundamental component for analyzing data. The paper also discusses how Enriched Distribution Networks (EDNs) and the denotational semantics of the BW language, which is part of the Sollya project, use this type to describe HMMs, especially in the context of finding the most likely explanation for a given observation. The paper also addresses the issue of dealing with infinite model states by proposing the use of a type called a quotient type, which can be used to describe and work with such types of models in a clean and effective manner. The paper also explains the issue of dealing with the issue of dealing with the lack of compositionality in HMMs and other types of Markov models, as well as proposing the use of a type called the distribution monad, which has a version with a type constructor that takes a type constructor as an argument and returns a type constructor that can be used to describe such types of models in a clean and effective manner. We explore the relationship between statistically nonlocal behavior and coherent patterns in turbulent fluid dynamics, such as vortex rings and anticyclones in homogenous expansions. These structures maintain their integrity due to the self-organization of the fluid's velocity field, which is driven by the conservation of quantities with long-term stability. The interaction between near and far-scale motion, facilitated by nonlinear dynamics, leads to the collapse of the velocity distribution and the subsequent formation of coherent structures. The effect of nonlocality is observed when the velocity field is affected by distant scales, not immediately adjacent to its point of measurement. In conventional Eulerian observations, the velocity at a given point is determined by the conditions immediately surrounding it, resulting in the loss of coherent patterns and the generation of random, nonlocal behavior, such as turbulence in fully chaotic flow conditions. However, by operating at a more refined scale, the significance of nonlocal interactions becomes apparent, enabling the detection of coherent patterns even at small distances. The presentation will demonstrate two numerical simulations that illustrate this relationship: (1) the initial formation of coherent patterns within a turbulent velocity field, and (2) the identification of already existing coherent structures down to the most detailed scales. These experiments were conducted as part of the "First Workshop on Geophysical Scales" held at the Woods Hole Laboratory in 2021. The results have also been published in an article titled "Coherent Patterns in Turbulence: From Turbulent Statistics to the Formation of Coherent Structures and Back?" in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics, Volume 933, Issue 2, 2021. The study has also been presented at multiple international conferences including the 25th Symposium on Geophysical & Space Environmental Physics held in July 2021 in Cambridge, as well as the 3I International Conference on Computational Methods in Engineering & Sciences in September 2020 in Barcelona. The work was accomplished while participating in the 2021 Woods Hole Laboratory Summer Program organized by Prof. Piero R. Paoletti. This model, called the 'Universal Folding Model' or 'UFM,' determines a nuclear interaction potential by folding the nuclear density distribution of one nucleus with another, independent of the energies involved. The potential's parameters are then calculated using a least squares fit to the available differential cross-section data across different energy levels. The UFM has been successfully tested using a wide range of differential cross-section data from various nuclear reactions. The model also enables the determination of the real part of the nuclear interaction potential and the nuclear density distribution of a non-folding nucleus involved in the reaction, as illustrated through examples with the systems 16,17,18,19,28,29,30 Ne on 40,56,58,62,64 Cu and 16,17,18,19,28,29,30 Ne targets. We utilize $T$, $A$, and $d$ as primary parameters to calculate the free energy of the system by integrating over the plate the stress-energy-momentum tensor derived by Brown and Maclay. Both thermodynamic regimes, $kTd/\hbar$ much larger or smaller than $1/\sqrt{ kd}$, are explored, as well as the Casimir's plate entropy in both scenarios, with a key limitation being that all the assumptions underlying Casimir's theory must be satisfied for this analysis to apply. We specifically compute various thermodynamic properties of the system, including heat capacity and entropy, as functions of temperature, temperature disparity with the thermal reservoir, distance between the walls, and system area. Furthermore, we investigate the Lionville-Rogowski phenomenon, where a system in thermal equilibrium undergoes a transition from a temperature $T_1$ to a temperature $T_2$ via a non-temperature-dependent distance variation between the walls. The results show that this process is characterized by two conditions: a temporary, negative specific heat and a specific heat disproportionate to the distance variation. Additionally, in the context of a system expanding isothermally, we compute the work performed and related efficiency factors, while in the context of a system contracting isothermally, we assess various indicators of irreversibility, including the second law strength and relevant factors. In accordance with the given general expression for the plate entropy when $kTd/\hbar < 1$, we derive a specific value for this entropy in both scenarios, as determined by Lionville-Rogowski's analysis. The results indicate that this entropy displays proportional relationships with the relevant temperature and distance, while also decreasing with an increase in the relevant temperature or system area, where the magnitude of the plate entropy shows a square root relationship with the relevant temperature and distance, in addition to an exponential relationship with the relevant temperature disparity with the thermal reservoir. The findings presented in this study indicate that a unique thermodynamic behavior can be achieved at scales where Casimir's effects can be observed, where certain patterns may need to be revised and others may require additional assumptions and a quantum field theory approach, particularly for small system sizes where quantized states may become significant. Despite the limitations of existing 2D image-based deep learning-based point cloud registration methods, our approach overcomes these constraints by converting 3D point clouds into 2D Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) maps using Normal Distribution Transform. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given the diverse languages involved, researchers have faced the challenge of 
overcoming the language barrier in code-mixing research. To tackle this issue, 
they have employed methods relying on linguistic rules and statistical approaches 
to analyze individual languages independently, then combine the results. 
Notably, neural network-based algorithms have proven highly effective in this area. 
To build on this success, researchers have adapted positional encoding methods, 
originally proposed in transformer architectures to model sequential data, to 
account for the varying language setups in code-mixed texts. To address this 
issue, we propose a dynamic positional encoding framework that can adapt to 
different language configurations and varying word orders across languages. 
Our framework incorporates a switching mechanism to determine the positional 
encoding based on the language used in the given text. Our experiments confirm 
that our approach performs exceptionally well on code-mixed datasets, especially when 
designed to handle multiple language combinations. Our results further indicate that 
our algorithm surpasses rule-based approaches when evaluated across multiple 
scenarios. We also showcase the effectiveness of our approach in two specific 
applications, code-mixing detection and sentiment analysis, demonstrating 
substantial improvements over alternative methods. We make our code available 
online for the benefit of future researchers.

This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In the field of autonomous driving and robotics, motion planning often relies on map-based constraints provided by a global planner. However, existing methods are often unsuccessful without pre-compiled maps or where environmental maps become outdated due to sudden changes like traffic congestion, roadblocks, or construction. Triangulation-based methods are viable alternatives but have limitations in dynamic environments. In an effort to improve upon this, we have devised a novel method using a sequence of spatial channels that accommodate multiple triangulation-based structures, serving as spatial boundaries for navigation in unstructured environments. Our approach is tested and compared with other triangulation-based methods on synthetic and real-world scenarios from an autonomous driving dataset. We demonstrate that our technique results in a more consistent, efficient, and collision-free motion plan compared to existing methods, including higher global planner success rates, faster planning times, and a reduction in triangulation failures. Our experimental findings also show that our method performs as well as traditional techniques in optimal cases, thereby offering a more versatile and dynamic navigation solution. Our technique is made publicly available at https://github.com/SafeAndLocal/spatial_constraint_generation. Our code is written in Python, compatible with ROS 1, and incorporates the open-source mesh lab library for efficient use. Our data consists of an autonomous driving dataset from the Waymo dataset. Our results show promising prospects for the application of our technique in various areas, including but not limited to autonomous driving. In particular, our method could seamlessly integrate with existing navigation systems to improve upon global planner success rates, plan efficiency, and hardware efficiency. Our results also suggest that our method could effectively tackle various complex robotics challenges such as door openings, where triangulation-based methods have historically underperformed. Our work has the potential to contribute meaningfully to the advancement of safe and local research in autonomous driving and robotics. This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and map features within the database. A step-by-step camera relocalization process is then applied to determine camera pose. Moreover, this method incorporates a two-part feature descriptor, consisting of a learning-based component for standard images and an alternative component for surfel-based frames. In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an algorithm grounded in the group LASSO approach. Relative to the existing solutions, the proposed method achieves two key improvements: higher attainable sum-rate values and lower interference at inactive user devices. The paper further explores the computational feasibility and information-theoretic optimality of the group LASSO-based approach, with support provided by the results of numerical experiments. These findings demonstrate that the algorithm is capable of finding an approximate solution in a relatively short time and, as a consequence, LASSO-derived solutions can be considered as suboptimal but feasible alternatives to traditional algorithms. The paper also shows that the performance of the group LASSO approach can be enhanced by applying a simple iteration that involves updating the set of active user devices. The method is capable of reducing the interference at inactive user devices, thus making it a viable solution when user selection and precoding are to be performed concurrently. The findings of the numerical evaluations are supported by the results of a real-world experiment, with the paper highlighting its potential applications in this area. The key outcomes of the study are: First, the algorithm outperformed its competitors in terms of sum-rate values, with LASSO-derived solutions accounting for 82% to 100% of the total sum-rate obtained using the baseline solution. Second, the algorithm outperformed its competitors in terms of lower interference at inactive user devices. Third, the algorithm outperformed its competitors in terms of computational complexity, with the total computational cost roughly one-tenth of the baseline solution. Fourth, the algorithm outperformed its competitors in terms of recovery accuracy, with the LASSO-derived solution recovering all 20 signals in the dataset. What's more, the algorithm's accuracy can be considered as the best in the class when the signal-to-noise ratio is at a relatively high value of 20. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have a critical drawback: they assign pseudo-labels to any node in the graph without considering the local structure surrounding each target node, which is essential in graph-based learning. To address this issue, we propose InfoGNN, a new pseudo-labeling framework specifically designed for Graph Neural Networks operating under the constraints of very few labels. InfoGNN within the self-training cycle identifies the most influential graph structure for each target node by conducting a local graph exploration, which is then utilized to generate informative pseudo-labels with a customized contrastive learning technique. As a result, the model is able to achieve enhanced accuracy even with the imposition of label scarcity constraints. With comparison to the existing state-of-the-art methods, InfoGNN has been shown to significantly outperform these methods including GraphNN, which results in a performance improvement of 6.54, 11.38, and 12.33 percentage points when limited to 10, 20, and 50 labels respectively. Moreover, our framework allows for scalar control over the influence of graph structure and label accuracy, which makes it highly flexible. This approach involves investigating the convergence properties of the trajectories generated by an inertial dynamic with Tikhonov regularization, and we demonstrate that, as time tends towards infinity, the solution converges towards the minimum norm solution at a rate dependent on the Tikhonov parameter, as well as the eigenvalue distribution of the Hessian matrix's positive semi-definite part. The methods developed in the present study also possess strong convergence properties, analogous to the rate of convergence defined by the Lyapunov function, and can be observed in the numerical simulations provided. Consequently, we propose the introduction of a new class of convergence criteria rooted in the notions of weak and strong convergence, in order to generalize the prior rates of convergence identified in the literature. The convergence criteria allow for the representation of the object of interest, in this case the solution towards which the solution converges, in terms of the minimum norm within a closed and convex set. As an example of the practical applicability of the proposed new class of convergence criteria, we generalize the weak convergence criteria for the dynamical method, where the coefficient related to the Hessian matrix's negative semi-definite part is non-negative. The generalized convergence criteria are expected to facilitate the determination of the solution's weak convergence properties when addressing a hierarchical minimization issue. Consequently, we propose the introduction of a new class of dynamic minimum-time optimization problems, where we seek to minimize a convex function with a minimum norm in a hierarchical context, in addition to other applications of the generalized convergence criteria. Building upon our previous research \cite{Liu:2019xhn}, we examine the prospect of primordial black holes emerging from the second inflationary process caused by the curvaton's oscillation. Utilizing the mathematical representation of the classical field tracker solution, we derive an expression for the primordial black hole mass and confirm that it is consistent with both Planck 2018 data and combined results from the Cosmic Microwave Background and large-scale structure observations. Furthermore, we illustrate that the variation in the primordial black particle mass is primarily due to the variation in the oscillation frequency, and a higher inflationary power spectrum leads to a greater frequency variation. In addition, we demonstrate that the variation in the black hole mass is primarily caused by the variation in the oscillation scale rather than the variation in the sound speed. Finally, we estimate the quantity of dark matter that can be accounted for by the primordial black holes formed from the second inflationary process for two distinct models featuring a sharp feature in the primordial power spectrum, and we find that the upper limits on the contribution of these black holes to the dark matter are 0.12 and 0.22, respectively. The curves that represent the relationship between the primordial black particle mass and the model parameter $r$ for the two models are also provided and explained in the context of future experiments to verify quantum gravity effects through the measurement of primordial black holes. The main conclusion of our investigation is that the variation in the primordial black particle mass is primarily caused by the variation in the oscillation scale rather than the variation in the classical field tracker solution. The potential relevance of our findings to the low-scale gravity scenario and the monkey trap problem is also discussed. A detailed explanation of our method for determining the quantity of dark matter accounted for by the primordial black holes is provided in the appendix of our study. The equations that represent the relationship between the primordial black particle mass and various parameters in the two models are derived in the appendix of our paper. To achieve this goal, our team has developed a sophisticated framework that integrates a pre-trained transformer model, as well as a dataset enriched with the linguistic and stylistic characteristics of artificially generated headlines. Through a process involving under-sampling, our approach has demonstrated significant improvements in handling imbalanced datasets. Moreover, our findings suggest that pre-trained transformer-based models are more effective than other text representation techniques in addressing the issue of imbalance and enhancing model performance. Experimental results indicate that the proposed system, which relies on pre-trained models and a preprocessed dataset, achieves impressive accuracy and F1 scores on imbalanced datasets, surpassing previous methods that rely on character-level encoding. For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for portfolio allocation, but a limitation of this approach is that it fails to account for short-term events and cannot replicate such scenarios in historical scenarios. In this study, a novel Autoencoding Conditional Generative Adversarial Network model was proposed to generate diverse short-term portfolios from historical data. Initially, an autoencoder network separates both the trends and discrepancies in the data, while a conditional GAN network generates various scenarios with identical trends by varying the discrepancies. Multiple methods were used to train the model, including the use of losses to promote diverse portfolios and a method to evaluate the validity of generated portfolios. Simulation results show that this model can effectively generate portfolios with diverse returns while maintaining a reasonable level of risk. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the utility of this model by generating portfolios for real investors, effectively replicating both the strategies of two renowned investors for picking stocks. This model is available for practical use on GitHub at https://github.com/zhangruotong/AcGAN4Portfolio. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.16242.

A groundbreaking method utilizing Bayesian neural networks demonstrates strong classification capabilities for classifying Fermi-LAT blazar types. In this study, we address the limitations of point-sources being categorized into BL Lacertae objects and Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars. Following an exhaustive examination of their differences, we encounter challenges in distinguishing them, prompting us to explore advanced machine learning techniques. Recent research has highlighted the effectiveness of Bayesian neural networks in understanding the uncertainty of machine learning models, a critical aspect in astronomical applications. We merge datasets from the Third Catalog of Active Galactic Nuclei and the Fermi-LAT catalog to identify blazars, leading to the analysis of a comprehensive $4\mu$sky area dataset. We implement two Bayesian neural network models as a composite score method to classify blazars and estimate their relationship using likelihood ratios and cumulative distribution functions. The results indicate that BSOLS scores demonstrate a strong correlation with the spectral index $\gamma$, while FSRQ/BL Lac correlations show slight deviations as $\gamma$ increases. We observe minimal statistical residuals after combining the classes of FSRQs and BL Lacs, suggesting the efficacy of our proposed method in categorizing blazars. The models developed in this study are expected to contribute significantly to the classification of future Fermi-LAT datasets, particularly for single-object of view studies and future radio surveys. Furthermore, we provide recommended classification thresholds for future research and potential follow-up studies with the Cypress mission. Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking, 
fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this content remains inaccessible to many users, 
despite available solutions that aim to reduce this form of exclusion. Our research 
involved surveying 258 social media users and interviewing 20 participants, with 8 of 
them having visual impairments, to understand their perceptions of online content 
and how support tools are utilized. Our analysis of the results reveals that 
platforms' efforts are inadequate, and that mainstream users often aren't aware 
of accessible practices. By exploring the views of end-users on accessible 
practices, barriers they face, and motivating factors, we also suggest further 
approaches to boost user engagement and raise awareness about accessibility. 

Ultimately, enhancing user experience and promoting social inclusion depend on 
strategically addressing these key aspects. Our findings suggest that future 
interventions should be grounded in a more profound comprehension of social 
participation from the perspective of the user, and that content authoring 
policies should strive to balance creativity with inclusivity. Moreover, we 
propose that facilitating the sharing of experiences between users, especially 
those with diverse backgrounds and skill sets, could aid in promoting 
cross-field learning and foster a more inclusive environment, ultimately leading 
to a culture of accessibility. 

This research aims to contribute to the advancement of both theoretical and 
practical research on accessibility by shedding light on social media's complex 
dynamic of user-generated content and social participation. Our results are also 
meant to inspire designers and researchers to develop more effective strategies to 
increase awareness about accessibility and foster a more inclusive 
environment, ultimately enhancing user engagement and social inclusion. 

This paper specifically explores the dynamic of user-generated content and 
social participation on social media, while a companion paper delves into 
accessibility and video content. Our work was funded by a CHI 2022 Late Breaking

In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations using tensors and demonstrate the equivalence of three formulations within this framework. The tensor representation enables efficient computation and analysis of hypergraphs, allowing for an alternative interpretation of famous hypergraph problems, such as the strong product of hypergraphs and bipartite hypergraph colorings. Based on this framework, we formulate and solve the maximum weight bipartite hypergraph coloring problem, achieving a constant factor approximation for specific cases and a randomized approximation ratio of 2 - o(1) for general hypergraphs. Additionally, we identify a hypergraph property associated with the tensor spectrum, as well as a method to construct universal hypergraphs within this framework. The results presented demonstrate the value of tensor-based methods for analyzing hypergraphs and their potential applications in both classic problems and novel domains. A novel computational strategy called Action-CSA is introduced, enabling the global exploration of reaction pathways via optimization of the Onsager-Machlup action using conformational space annealing. Compared to other sampling approaches, Action-CSA has proven to be both efficient and flexible. Action-CSA has been successfully tested on three challenging systems: (1) an intramolecular cyclization involving a large conformational space and high energy barriers; (2) a multistate process among vinylidene isomers on the cyclopentadienyl ring; and (3) a vinyllogous nitrosation reaction with a large and complex energy landscape. Results from these tests have shown that Action-CSA is able to find dominant reaction pathways even when other sampling methods fail. Notably, Action-CSA has identified a long-suspected multistate mechanism of vinyllogous nitrosation that had previously been hypothesized but lacked concrete evidence. Overall, Action-CSA presents a valuable and efficient method for uncovering reaction mechanisms that cannot be explored through existing simulation methods. Moreover, Action-CSA enables the systematic evaluation and efficient generation of transition pathways via multiple conformational sampling, potentially opening up new applications in designing reaction pathways based on prior art. Action-CSA's conformational space annealing components are equally adaptable and could find uses in tasks such as protein folding, structure determination from simulations, and the design of molecular structures. Notably, Action-CSA's efficiency and effectiveness in determining transition pathways are likely a first in their field. Notably, Action-CSA's approach is compatible with potential future extensions, such as the exploration of phase space. Notably, Action-CSA's approach is primarily based on dynamic simulations, but it could be combined with static methods such as density functional theory, potentially yielding a very powerful tool for chemical analysis. Action-CSA and its predicted applications are discussed in further detail. Future work is suggested to explore the potential uses of Action-CSA in designing molecular structures and investigating phase space transitions. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. The proposed method effectively boosts schema alignment without relying on additional data, and our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Charwery/auxISQL.

- Two value filling strategies are presented to compensate for existing zero-shot parsers' limitations on value filling in synthesized SQL.

dialogue state tracking are designed for processing tokenized text and cannot 
handle the ambiguity of speech directly. We propose an ASR ambiguity model 
based on Confusion Networks to address the speech-to-text ambiguity in AST 
training, providing a more consistent input condition. Since the model relies 
on Confusion Networks, it can be efficiently trained on existing datasets 
without requiring any speech or language data. We have tested the model's

1.24% improvement in overall F1-score compared to the baseline, when using the

The analysis of ESAR (Edge Sounder Array) measurements in the JET tokamak during H-mode reveals the frequent existence of persistent, low-frequency edge eigenmodes with characteristics such as localized, high-frequency turbulence, edible frequencies, and a perceived stationary origin. Two distinct types of these palm tree modes have been identified: those associated with the edge accretion rate and the soft X-point. The specifications of these modes, including their frequencies and parallel propagation velocities, suggest their possible connection with the edge of the scrape-off layer. Furthermore, research demonstrates that the palm tree modes may hinder the formation of the H-mode edge current sheet, thereby facilitating ACMS (Acoustic Edge Current Drive) injection. The interaction between the ACMS injections and the palm tree modes has the potential to either accelerate or reduce their frequencies. The discovery of these modes presents an opportunity to examine their underlying physics and whether their presence depends on specific experimental settings, such as the edge accretion rate, plasmatic fuel, and magnetic topology. If these modes prove recurrent in other devices, their study could lead to a deeper understanding of their origins within the scrape-off layer and their possible links to turbulence-driven transport. The existence of these modes in various edge conditions suggests that the palm tree modes may be a widespread phenomenon, potentially offering valuable insights into generalized physical phenomena. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Neighbor Classifier (NNC). This comparison showcases that the basic NNC approach achieves comparable performance to cutting-edge continual learning methods on the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 datasets. The findings hint at a potential shift in the direction of the continual learning research community, urging caution when using costly and complex models in continual learning environments. As social media grows in influence, the need to curb the spread of hateful content on platforms like Twitter and YouTube becomes increasingly crucial. The toxicity of such content not only damages relationships but also can also incite violent behavior, exacerbating social tensions and fostering social divides. Previous studies have primarily focused on detecting hateful language, typically relying on a narrow set of indicators such as profanity and racial slurs, despite their clear limitations in capturing the full spectrum of hateful language. In contrast, we take a more comprehensive approach, analyzing both the textual content and visual components of social media posts, such as user profiles and images. We incorporate numerical and categorical metadata, such as followers and post times, into our model, allowing us to explore the interpretability of our approach. By doing so, we hope to increase the accuracy of our model and illustrate the significance of visual elements in complex multi-modal hate detection. The proposed model outperforms existing baselines in terms of Accuracy, Macro F1, and F1, showcasing its potential as a reliable hate detection model on social media platforms. We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory neurons causes a shift from synchronized activity to asynchronous, while in excitatory networks, this leads to oscillatory states. In gap junction coupled networks, narrowing the in-degree distribution of excitatory neurons results in a transition from synchronized to asynchronous states. These insights provide valuable guidelines to experimenters in designing networks with tailored behavioral patterns. Additionally, we link the effects observed in random networks to the effects seen in more structured networks, where in- and out-degrees are determinate. Our work highlights the importance of understanding the effects of network architecture in neural networks.  This article is part of a special Issue: The mathematical physics of neuroscience. numerous approaches being explored. Most APR methods typically utilize syntactic
elements from input outputs to generate repairs, focusing on minor syntax deviations.
However, such approaches are often prone to high repair failure rates, mainly due
to their lack of understanding of program semantics. On the other hand, state-of-the-art
approach, CodePatch, demonstrates relatively low failure rates by leveraging
adversarially sampled program patches. In this paper, we take a step further by
exploring the patch sampling technique. By reformulating patch sampling as a
optimization problem, we aim to discover more effective repair methods. A close
examination of our reformulation reveals that the current sample density of the
search space in CodePatch is biased. Therefore, we propose an alternative search
density model and develop a reinforcement learning strategy to guide the sampling
process. By implementing our method in DeepDP, we are able to generate patches with
a higher degree of appropriateness. Moreover, our results on the Lang2 and Method2
benchmarks show that DeepDP achieves an impressive repair failure rate of 1.1%,
outperforming the state-of-the-art approach CodePatch with a significant margin of
20.1%. A thorough analysis of our approach also reveals that the search density model
has the potential to be universally applied to various APR techniques, making it a
promising candidate for improving the effectiveness of APR methods. A A pre-trained

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied across multiple domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions can severely hinder GNN's dependence on inter-node data exchange. To overcome this limitation, this thesis explores the application of decentralized inference in GNNs, specifically within wireless communication systems, by incorporating edge computing at various nodes and focusing on two primary issues: (i) enhancing GNN model expression using matrix multiplication, and (ii) resolving the dependency between inter-node data exchanges during prediction. Our innovative solutions, respectively, leverage reduced matrix transfer and prediction-stage data exchange, both significantly boosting prediction efficiency. Furthermore, we have also adapted a GNN-based device detection mechanism which can be utilized by 5G cellular networks and future Tactile Internet services to control human-related inputs, such as touch, in cases where original signals cannot be transmitted due to restricted feedback bandwidth. In this scenario, our decentralized detection approach enables devices to obtain necessary information from their neighbors, thereby facilitating reliable inference. Overall, our current implementations of decentralized inference in GNNs result in notable performance improvements, with significant reductions in information exchange and processing times. As such, this technique has the potential to effectively utilize local data and facilitate efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. Finally, additional research opportunities have been identified for further exploration of decentralized inference in GNNs. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and facilitates data processing. To account for respiratory variations, sequence adaptation is achieved through online adjustments in sampling points and mid-acquisition trigger times for the subsequent half-acquisitions. The sequence parameters for sampling points are predicted offline via chest-wall kernel correlation, while trigger times are adjusted online via a respiratory sensor that measures period length. The proposed sequence is evaluated using phantom and abdominal imaging data collected at 1.5 T and 3.0 T. Comparative studies and assessment of methods for reconstructing images from raw data, including multiband and multiband with model-based reconstruction, are also conducted to determine the optimal reconstruction technique. Our research demonstrates that rCASPR-rTRSE can produce high-quality, motion-compensated T2-weighted images in as little as four to five minutes with good signal-to-noise ratio, accuracy in assessing abdominal organ positioning and organ volume, and improved eye-tracking results in radiology applications. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving enhanced results on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100. The implementation details are publicly accessible at our website. Our study reveals that model compression can be effectively treated as a task of preserving and transferring information flow, thereby setting the stage for future research in this area. Furthermore, our findings indicate that incorporating entity chains allows for more effective hallucination control, and we were able to improve faithfulness of generated summaries by prompting the model to omit irrelevant information. Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behaviors, suggesting the need for accurate measurement of entrainment patterns in conversations. Instead of relying on traditional, rule-based approaches that may struggle with real-world conversation complexities, this paper introduces a mathematical model to quantify entrainment by analyzing the statistical properties of speech patterns. The model's effectiveness is verified through comparisons with existing measurement methods in multiple conversation scenarios, highlighting its advantages in efficiently capturing fine-grained entrainment features and effectively distinguishing between various levels of vocal synchronization. By applying this measurement approach, individual entrainment characteristics can be identified and evaluated in two real-world datasets. The proposed measurement method is available for public use on the GitHub platform. The paper includes supplementary materials, including videos, animation files, a PDF summary, and associated code. The model utilizes two key statistical measures: the allelic association measure of Nadeau et al. (2018) to capture within-conversation moments of vocal synchronization and the temporal autocorrelation of speech patterns. The model's performance is demonstrated in two conversation domains - individuals conversing with strangers and pairs interacting during a role-playing task - where it successfully distinguishes between various levels of vocal synchronization. The study also demonstrates the potential drawbacks of the temporal autocorrelation measure in predicting entrainment characteristics, especially in cases where the temporal autocorrelation of speech patterns is not strongly related to the level of vocal synchronization. The research highlights several future directions for measuring vocal entrainment, including leveraging advanced time-series analysis models, such as the self-organizing features technique, to capture the underlying properties of vocal synchronization, as well as exploring the connection between vocal entrainment and the mental processes underlying social communication. The proposed measurement approach is expected to contribute to the development of system models that can predict vocal synchronization in social interactions, which in turn may lead to the development of more accurate and automated social robots. A primary challenge arises from the presence of a pre-existing cavitation, resulting in a velocity field with a particular characteristic at the grounding line, thus rendering the Stokes variational inequality neither semicoercive nor variational. To tackle this challenge, a modified approach has been developed by employing a finite element method with optimal error estimates, taking into account the properties of the associated Stokes problem. This has been achieved by employing a novel localization technique, particularly suited for use in conjunction with the finite element method. with a discussion emerging on the optimal task for pre-training.
Some researchers suggest that a task that utilizes multiple-object hints may
offer benefits, such as promoting spatial coherence, for image analysis.
We investigate this idea by comparing the effects of pre-training on image
segmentation tasks with two approaches: using classification as a single-object
hint or using depth estimation as a multi-object hint. Our experiments,
carrying over to other state-of-the-art methods, demonstrate that employing
depth estimation as a pre-training task leads to superior results when the aim
is semantic segmentation. When utilizing the same architecture and data, our
findings show that incorporating depth estimation results in an enhancement of up
to 2% mIoU over classification-based pre-training on the Cityscapes dataset.
We also observe that employing depth estimation leads to more stable convergence
during pre-training. Consequently, our study suggests that utilizing depth
estimation as a pre-training task from a multi-object viewpoint may be a more
effective method in comparison to classification for achieving better results

This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses, especially in studies involving random fields. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, the theoretical and computational feasibility of the Euler characteristic make it an attractive intermediate step for multi-variable topological analysis. We demonstrate its practicality by using artificial datasets and a real-world example involving diabetic retinopathy detection from retinal images. Our results encompass theoretical, methodological, and practical aspects. Firstly, we examined the connection between the Euler characteristic and self-avoiding walks. Secondly, we developed a method to estimate the Euler characteristic using point coverage of a sample. Finally, we tested this method on diabetes-related features in retinal images, employing a binary classification framework that utilizes image context for retinal surface segmentation. Our findings show that the Euler characteristic offers a simple yet effective solution for basic topological analysis in high-dimensional spaces. Moreover, it serves as an efficient and feasible method for visual and quantitative analysis of irregular networks. Our proposed approach is available as open-source software for general use. The provided code can be directly applied to any multi-variable space for characterizing datasets. It is also compatible with the DyRENA suite, which is specifically designed for dynamic retinal networks. Therefore, the code is particularly suitable for applications involving retinal image analysis. Our study integrates theoretical, methodological, and practical contributions to the field of topological data analysis in high-dimensional spaces. While the results are primarily theoretical, they are accompanied by a comprehensive evaluation of a methodological and computational approach. Moreover, we successfully applied the Euler characteristic to a real-world image processing and classification task, which is a critical area of study in machine learning and pattern recognition. Our approach is not only applicable to retinal imaging but can also be extended to other domains, such as geometry, material science, and other multi-variable analysis fields. Unfortunately, the provided code does not support artificial dataset generation, which is something that could be included in future enhancements. Similarly, the study does not explore the use of machine learning as an advanced learning method for topological data, which is an area of potential future research. The main problem with the current approach is that the results are based on a simple topological invariant, which may not be as powerful as employing more advanced invariants like homology in high-dimensional spaces. Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and learning from errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for advanced driving education using the IBM Deep Reinforcement Learning platform. Our innovative approach leverages a cutting-edge policy gradient algorithm to train self-driving vehicles in conjunction with a cutting-edge monocular object detector. The integration of a rule-based system enables smoother learning by incorporating capabilities such as automatic steering, throttle, and brake functions. To guarantee safe learning, we employed Congestion Free Simulation Optimization, a parallel optimization algorithm enabling the downscaling of scenarios to balance exploration and representation with local optimization of rewards in large open environments. With this framework, the self-driving car can safely navigate complex routes, handle congested traffic, and respond to novel situations. In line with the principles of model-driven reinforcement learning, we have successfully trained the vehicle to perform a sequence of actions in diverse environments without exposing it to excessive risk. The final model has been exported and deployed on real-world systems. Our work marks the successful application of Deep reinforcement learning in the automotive industry. It sheds light on the critical factors that contribute to its effectiveness and presents a versatile framework for the education of advanced driving algorithms. Moreover, the integration of a cutting-edge object detector, which facilitates the learning process by providing spatial object coordinates, has notably improved the algorithm's efficiency. In particular, we have observed a dramatic 99% reduction in the number of required training steps to navigate complex environments and achieve high scores on the benchmark track. Consequently, the framework presents a cutting-edge solution for the education of autonomous vehicles, which can be adapted and fine-tuned via the incorporation of diverse detector architectures to enhance performance and efficiency. Ultimately, the framework has paved the way for the successful deployment of autonomous driving algorithms on real-world systems. As a consequence, PEA's search capability is restricted, with certain ants being assigned more CPU time and thus more opportunities to create offspring. To address this problem, we introduce a novel parent selection strategy that takes into account the duration of previous evaluations. Our experimental findings, conducted across 12 numerical test functions, compare the newly developed Frequency-based Parent Selection (FPS) against a First-come-First-Served (FCFS) method within the framework of Asynchronous Parallel Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithms (APMEA). According to our findings, the highest improvement is observed in the IPS-S2 module. Despite the importance of understanding the effective Floquet generator of a CPT symmetric time-periodic Lindblad generator, a comprehensive theoretical framework remains elusive. Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily rely on surrogate models to generate explanations for specific instances, but a major limitation is that they struggle to provide insight into the factors that contribute to similar predictions across multiple instances. In response, we propose the GPE - Graph Parameterized Explainer, a novel approach that uses an interpretable model to explain GNN predictive decisions. By adjusting a key hyperparameter across a range of integer values, GPE helps to identify the significant graph structural factors that contribute to a model's predictive accuracy for a given instance or group of similar instances. Our extensive testing confirms that GPE effortlessly identifies relevant graph structural factors for inductive problems and can easily incorporate multiple factors. Moreover, as the explainer's hyperparameter increases, the explanations provided by GPE become progressively more precise and focused. In our view, GPE offers a valuable and practical solution for enhancing transparency in complex GNN systems. Our code is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/ruishao-tsai/GPE.
