The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore its development and composition, we examined archival X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton, examining the dynamic cluster state and searching for gas substructures. Its X-ray brightness distribution exhibits no evident disruption except for an elongation in the North-East to South-West direction. We applied the unsharp masking technique and calculated the morphology parameters to assess disturbance levels. These analyses identified a South-West substructure located at approximately 1 arcminute from the core, indicating the system may possess a quiet core but turbulent surroundings that potentially pump energy to the detected radio halo. Its dynamic state may indicate that this system has not reached dynamic equilibrium. Further detailed dynamic cluster information was obtained using a likelihood-based estimation of the cluster's dark matter distribution, while the X-ray gas fraction was calculated to determine the fraction of cluster mass comprised by hot gas. This hot gas fraction was used to estimate the mechanical energy transferred to the ICM through turbulent motion and relativistic particles. This information will aid in better understanding this peculiar system's formation and evolution. This research utilized data from the Chandra and XMM-Newton observatories, with all related materials available online. Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, was developed and has demonstrated superior performance on various benchmark datasets. In this work, the linear component of the LMU is optimized, resulting in a simplified variant that can be trained in parallel, thus overcoming the obstacle of GPU training limitations on RNNs. Our modification allows training to proceed up to 200 times faster. Furthermore, the performance of our model is evaluated on seven benchmarks in comparison to the original LMU and several other prominent deep networks. Our models consistently achieve superior results on these datasets and are particularly notable for their ability to handle low signal-to-noise ratio data effectively. Additionally, the performance of our models is explored in the context of sequence classification tasks involving long sequences. Our analysis reveals that the streamlined LMU is a more efficient solution for such tasks in comparison to the original LMU and other deep neural networks. Our code is openly available for review on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/prajithvm/journal CLUB/LMU/tree/20221109-parallel-LMU. The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects for directly detecting dark matter particles weighing less than GeV/c$^2$. Its ability to analyze numerous isotopes within its target material is an advantage in exploring dark matter interactions. This research focuses on dark matter interactions with $^{6}$Li protons and neutrons, made feasible through updated nuclear matrix calculations for this specific lithium isotope. By utilizing data collected by a CRESST prototype using LiAlO$_2$ and tested above ground in Munich, Germany, we demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating $^{6}$Li into our calculations to improve our detection of spin-dependent interactions between dark matter and neutrons, particularly significant for particles weighing less than 1 GeV/c$^2$ where improvements of over two orders of magnitude are seen compared to previously published results with the same data. The addition of $^{6}$Li also enables us to explore interaction possibilities with dark matter and the neutron-proton spin, offering new avenues for research. Our current findings include limits on dark matter-nucleon interactions, with particularly stringent limits for the dark matter-neutron interaction when the dark matter mass is near 1 GeV/c$^2$. This research was carried out as part of a collaborative effort between the CRESST and MARE Collaboration. The former is based at the Austrian Research and Education Institute of STKI in Graz and the latter is a new partnership focused on researching the properties of MeV dark matter particles, based within a group at the Max-Planck-Institute in Munich. The results were obtained through an analysis of a 229 gram sample utilizing a heat and emulsion technique within a 50-ppm range, with significant findings including the ability to detect the radioactive decay of $^{210}$Pt under conditions of particle radiation. This was achieved by studying interactions involving the decay of alpha particles and using simulations to understand the movement of particles within the detector to pinpoint events within a three-dimensional space. The results from this analysis have significant implications for the research of dark matter particles weighing a single GeV for interactions with the neutron. By combining the use of multiple targets within the same experiment the collaboration has the potential to discover such particles. The results were established using data collected within a above ground prototype within a 50-ppm range for radiopurity. Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, an ill-posed problem, resolved by restricting either the image or a blur kernel representing blur. Differing from prior research, this study regulates the structure of the blur kernel. The kernel mixture concept utilizes Gaussian kernels with enhanced scale and orientation flexibility, producing a nearly non-parametric blur shape representation. The corresponding kernel scales are determined through a regression method based on deep learning, supplemented by a weak loss function tied to the latent image, thereby requiring no additional supervision. The results of experiments on both natural and man-made images demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository designated as blindeblurringkm. Furthermore, this research has been supported by funding from the China National Fund. Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance, however, struggles when dealing with failures or byzantine attacks, leading to the development of RCanopus. RCanopus enhances Canopus to not only tolerate various types of failures but also resist malicious activities by correctly identifying and accommodating multiple types of failures while maintaining agreement on such events. The formal verification of RCanopus's correctness has been achieved through creation of a two new formal models that combine network failures and byzantine attacks, and its implementation demonstrates a canopus performance with failure and byzantine attack protection. The evaluation of RCanopus shows it can manage up to 84M operations per second while still being able to manage failures on various distributed machine setups. The evaluation also shows that RCanopus has a canopus-like latency and is able to handle various types of failures with correctness on Amazon EC2 machines. The ability of RCanopus to manage various types of failures and byzantine attacks opens the door for it to be used in various canopus-based systems such as distributed databases and blockchains. The configuration of its failure detection and byzantine attack handling mechanisms can be adjusted based on the specific system it is being used for. Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, which examine linear transport properties, have yielded contrasting results when analyzing the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers. This inconsistency arose despite earlier research employing solely equilibrium experiments, not linear transport properties, indicating that one may be misled by data from the latter. In order to elucidate this discrepancy, this paper introduces a scenario in which neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods yield different results. The primary goal of this paper is to clarify that the bending modulus measured through linear transport properties is not necessarily indicative of the true Gaussian modulus when dealing with materials like lipid bilayers, particularly those affected by additives like cholesterol. The study suggests performing supplementary experiments to determine the correct relationship between the two moduli or employing experimental techniques that directly measure the elasticity of the material in question. The authors hope this information will contribute usefully to ongoing research and encourage experiments testing the impact of cholesterol on the 2-dimensional modulus of lipid bilayers. Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair of them using the same path simultaneously. Through an analysis based on weak values, we uncover inconsistencies in the description. By incorporating transversal modes and examining the emergence of correlations between path and traversal properties, we also investigate the rotational symmetry of the output pattern as an indicator of pairwise interactions. However, our analysis finds that the symmetry bears no evident connection to the probability of three particles exiting the interferometer together. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the apparent symmetry breaking in the output can be attributed to the analytical method employed rather than a physical phenomenon, and that similar features are present in scenarios involving classical particles displaying coherent interference. Ultimately, we propose that the original experiment's findings require further clarification through supplementary measurements, potentially involving techniques like quasiprobability distributions or hidden variable simulations. The relevance of quantum mechanics to this problem is already briefly discussed in the conclusion. 

The code for our analysis is available on github at https://github.com/TongBasu/pigeonhole_sciadv.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy resulting from approximations. This paper suggests an alternative by temporarily switching from an initial approximation to a more precise one, before applying the interpolation phase to improve overall accuracy. The proposed approach is theoretically justified and tested on a simple case study, which yielded substantial gains in precision for several different scenarios. The results show that, in general, the overall precision of the analysis is significantly improved when the more precise approximation is used during the upward phase correctly identified as such during the downward phase. However, when the analysis is unable to determine which phase is in progress, employing the more precise approximation can actually decrease overall precision in some cases where it is actually during the downward phase. Therefore, the paper suggests that such uncertainty should be resolved by ignoring the upward phase altogether and moving straight to the downward phase for maximum precision. The paper concludes with suggestions for future research. This extended abstract is a simplified version of the full technical report available at https://doc.inria.fr/dotclear.html#Hal-03492747.

Developing CS NLP systems is complicated by the scarcity of CS data, a problem that data augmentation can help mitigate. Research has primarily focused on English-Swahili and English-Spanish CS scenarios, leaving the case of Arabic-English CS (AR-EN) CS NLP unsolved. In contrast to other CS languages, Arabic presents unique challenges due to its highly inflected and template-based structure, as well as its distinct vocabulary and grammar compared to English. Given the scarcity of AR-EN CS data, we explore the feasibility of augmenting training data by conducting lexical replacements. Specifically, we investigate the potential of substituting Arabic words with their English equivalents, and vice versa, to create new CS examples. Employing a automated tool for this purpose, we analyze its performance using CS datasets in various domains, including a medical dataset and two Shift codeswitching datasets. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our augmented data approach on a CS word sense disambiguation task in a different context. Ultimately, we discuss the potential implications of our findings on CS NLP and offer recommendations for further study. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. In contrast, a subset of homeomorphisms that only reflect symmetry is topologically compact. Moreover, our results extend to include whitehead groups, their amalgamated free products over finite subgroups, and other related groups, encompassing surface braid groups and its analogous groups. These findings build on work by Dru\c{t}\'{i}k that identify which groups of homeomorphisms are topologically compact. In addition, our results align with existing works by Ghys and Le\'{o}nnis that deal with the Banach-Mazur property in groups of surface homeomorphisms. We also establish that certain groups of homeomorphisms have a Banach-Mazur property by combining our results with Burroughs, Dru\c{t}\'{i}k, Ferrad\`{o}s, et al.'s work. We further demonstrate that a Banach-Mazur property is maintained under the condition of a weak invariance of the surface's boundary. Ultimately, our results reveal that groups of homeomorphisms that fix the boundary are unique in having this property. To achieve this goal, our work involves developing new arguments as well as leveraging existing works, including those related to surface topology, the geometry of its group actions, the dynamics of its homeomorphisms, and the topology of its surface. We also explore other related questions in our research paper. We expect our findings to be of great value in the fields of topological dynamics, the geometry of groups, and the dynamics of homeomorphisms. To make our work more accessible, our accompanying supplementary material has been provided with all the relevant details. A fundamental concept in addressing these problems is the mesh, composed of basic elements - vertices, edges, and faces. To gain insight into a wide range of problems, researchers and practitioners employ the mesh framework to build static and interactive models. A core operation for manipulating and understanding meshes is the edge split, which allows the edge structure to change by creating a new vertex. Unlike other data structures, the mesh can represent complex, irregular patterns. For centuries, the mesh has been utilized in applications, including cartography and sculpting, due to its ability to accurately depict complex shapes. Additionally, the mesh's robustness and low implementation cost have made it an ideal choice. A specific type of mesh, the planar mesh, stands out by allowing all its faces to have a specific geometry with three natural components - edges, curves, and lines. A notable property of the mesh is that its elements can be used to describe a wide range of geometric concepts. A few basic operations on the mesh's structure, including edge split and edge collapse, allow researchers to modify the mesh's topology. In turn, the mesh's elements can be employed to build static and interactive models. Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming certain conditions about the outcomes of our actions.  A key condition,
known as Lipschitz smoothness, ensures that small changes in behavior lead to
similar results.  However, this condition is often too restrictive for real-world
scenarios.  In this paper, we propose a milder version of this condition,
appropriate for situations where small biases don't significantly impact our
decisions.  Our new condition enables us to develop a broad range of task types
based on metrics and rewards, while ensuring that our learning algorithm remains
efficient and effective.  We test our proposal on a variety of complex tasks, and
show that our method can effectively tackle these challenges with minimal adjustments.  Interestingly, our results suggest that Coarse-Lipschitz values may provide performance benefits even in situations where more precise estimates are feasible.  Overall, our approach expands the range of conditions under which efficient, effective reinforcement learning is possible.  A particular consequence of our paper is that the EXPLICO framework, initially designed with low variance assumptions, can also achieve strong results in more relaxed settings - thus demonstrating that the learning algorithm itself is not the primary factor contributing to these conditions.  Our implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/jase-clarkson/explico/tree/rl_in_metric_spaces.  Our paper appears to be the first to propose a condition as mild as Coarse-Lipschitz for reinforcement learning in metric spaces, and also the first to use categorical domain changes in that setting.  Our results suggest a number of promising research avenues, including an analysis of Coarse-Lipschitz values in more precise terms, an exploration into making these conditions almost completely independent of the action choice, and an investigation into whether the learning algorithm can itself produce such conditions.  Our first contribution involves showing that our Coarse-Lipschitz condition is feasible in a setting where low variance assumptions were previously known to be sufficient.  Ultimately, our paper challenges assumptions about the requirements of the EXPLICO framework and its cousins, and suggests a number of ideas for how these assumptions may be relaxed with interesting results. In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a top priority. However, commonly used methods such as the finite element method and finite volume method are often prone to inaccuracies and artifacts, like Gibbs oscillations, particularly when approximating complex characteristics. This necessitates the development of advanced post-processing techniques, like mesh-free methods, that can handle complex geometries without altering the original solution data. However, implementing such techniques is often met with challenges in high-dimensional spaces. To address this issue, we introduce a novel convex optimization-based filter that can be applied across various dimensions. This filter utilizes L1 regularization and is compatible with a broad range of discretization methods. Through theoretical analysis, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the solution. This is further demonstrated by performing numerous numerical simulations in 1D to 5D spaces, showing the efficacy of the proposed filter in creating smooth, accurate solutions while preserving user-specified function properties. Several mesh-free and finite element simulations are also highlighted to illustrate the practical application of the proposed filter in real-world scenarios. Lastly, we showcase the ability of the proposed filter to handle complex problems by performing simulations in 1D to 5D spaces for partial differential equations. This is particularly useful in scenarios like the simulation of compressible fluid interacting with incompressible fluid or the simulation of fluid interacting with a rigid body. To create smooth, non-singular velocity and density fields in such scenarios, we perform the simulations using the proposed filter while imposing the necessary physical constraints on the solution. Several mesh-free and finite element simulations are also highlighted to illustrate the practical application of the proposed filter in real-world scenarios. In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents often exhibit unpredictable behavior when faced with different social and environmental scenarios. This paper proposes a transfer learning method, known as Transfer Empowerment (TE), to address the social aspect of reinforcement learning. By modeling the unknown behavior of social counterparts as an unobservable Markov process, TE develops an agent's ability to infer its impact on this Markov process and empower itself with the information gained from interactions. This self-instructional capability is achieved through the use of context-dependent intrinsic motivation and update rules, allowing the agent to adapt its behavior to maximize its expected empowerment return. As a result, TE enables the agent to develop a consistent approach to responding to its social counterparts, even in the face of changes in its own or social behavior. Using the Krahenberg flow control chip as a real-world example, we demonstrate TE's effectiveness in a variety of scenarios, including when the social dynamic is altered due to the introduction of noisy interactions, a differing sense of the agent's past behavior, and a change in priorities. Experimental results verify that TE provides a robust framework for addressing the unpredictable nature of multi-agent reinforcement learning settings. Furthermore, TE's effectiveness is shown in comparison to other state-of-the-art methods, including mutual information maximization, as well as a context-free empowerment approach, providing a meaningful baseline for comparison. The proposed approach is implemented using a variational autoencoder representation of the Markov process, allowing the integration of TE into a variety of MARL settings. As such, TE offers a versatile framework for addressing the complex social dynamics of multi-agent reinforcement learning settings. Implementation details are available at https://github.com/steve109/te_marl. A video illustration of the approach can be viewed at https://youtu.org/pzgU1G1R_zE. The information content of transfer empowerment presented in this study has been experimentally determined. Following the guidelines established by Amari and Lengerto, the distribution of transfer empowerment over the training dataset was first approximated. Using the Shannon entropy as the metric for information content, the proposed method was validated by showing that the average information content of transfer empowerment exhibits a direct correlation with the agent's expected transfer performance. This approach allows our method, known as LoFTR, to effectively find dense matches in low-texture regions where traditional detectors face difficulties. Experiment results on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods with significant margin and excels on visual localization tasks, topping rankings on two prominent benchmarks. Notably, our method can also serve as a preprocessor for object detection and as a detailed refinement step. Being purely based on deep learning and detector-free, LoFTR holds great potential for expanding to other computer vision areas. The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias in existing inversion methods. Employing a numerical phantom with a horn-shaped volume, the influence of viewpoint and signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) is examined. These experiments revealed that noise severely impacts the accuracy of calculating the magnetic field component parallel to the line-of-sight (Bpar), whereas determining Bperp systematically underestimates the actual value. This error becomes more pronounced with increasing SNR in a noise-dominated scenario. Various techniques to mitigate this bias were tested, and the results showed that adding random noise to parallax flux maps or utilizing a least squares optimization with a damping term performed better than straightforward corrections. Nevertheless, the most effective approach to reduce the bias is employing a total magnetic energy minimization (TME) technique, which naturally regulates Bpar and enhances the accuracy of Bperp measurements. This study primarily focuses on the bias in context of solar physics, specifically SDO/HMI, but the discussed techniques are widely applicable to other areas of imaging as well. Moreover, the inferred magnetic energy flux is shown to be resilient to noise, whereas the perpendicular field component remains susceptible to bias. Finally, the authors prescribe an adjustable calibration factor specific to each viewing angle to address the known noise-coupled bias in order to refine future forward modeling and reconstruction techniques. This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel-ICA implementations. To address this issue, we adapt the FastICA code in Python's scikit-learn library to accommodate various types of kernel transformations. By doing so, we make the kernel-ICA algorithm open-source and accessible for the first time. The proposed'm-ar-K-FastICA' approach utilizes the m-arcsinh kernel, which offers advantages in terms of its strong discriminability, minimal loss of information, and computational efficiency. The proposed approach also allows for learning a kernel-based metaticket that can be seamlessly integrated into existing workflows for data analysis. In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the dominant approach. Each ad impression resulting from user interaction is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids typically based on the value of the ad impression and optimal bid price. Nonetheless, existing methods are often hindered by the inability to systematically consider multiple factors when creating bids, resulting in potential losses for DSPs. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces an adaptive risk-averse bidding strategy specifically tailored for display advertising. Our new approach dynamically sets an upper limit on potential losses to mitigate uncertainty and includes two key components: 1) a user-specific temporal auction prediction model that relies on temporal features and includes the impact of previous wins and losses, and 2) a bidding strategy that dynamically adjusts bid prices based on predicted auction outcomes and a user's historical performance in auctions. Our method has been tested using real-world data and compared against top-performing state-of-the-art algorithms. Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of remotely generating Wigner negativity in one subsystem given another's specific measurement. Research has previously established that when Alice and Bob share a Gaussian state, Bob can create Wigner negativity in Alice's system through measurement, if and only if Bob has a shared Gaussian state with Wigner negativity, with Alice's measurement being non-classical. This study extends these findings to a scenario where the shared Gaussian state is not necessarily positive, with focused examination of cases involving two modes. It is determined that when Alice and Bob share a two-mode Gaussian state, where Bob can use measurement to create Wigner negativity in Alice's system, Bob also has the capability to use measurement to create this same nonclassical correlation. This study concludes that the condition of nonclassical correlation is necessary for remote Wigner negativity generation. Moreover, this study evaluates the distinct characteristics of quantum steerable and Wigner negativity in these systems. Notably, these two nonclassical properties can exist separately and may not always coincide, as seen in one of the studied cases. Nonetheless, when Wigner negativity in one system enables another, that system itself also has the potential to be quantum steerable, implying that these nonclassical properties are closely intertwined. Consequently, this system exhibits an unusual type of topological phase transition, distinguished by a linear progression of entanglement levels with respect to the entanglement length. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameterisation, derived from a joint posterior distribution derived from extreme value statistics. By transforming these parameters, they become independent and uniformly distributed within a specified range, facilitating easier exploration of the parameter space. We illustrate the effectiveness of this method in a simulation study and apply it to real-world data. The observed results support the use of parameter transformation for efficient exploration of the parameter space, particularly when employing Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Additionally, we demonstrate that this method is compatible with uncertainty quantification and prediction tasks. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, reducing a representation's loss through subtle, imperceptible modifications to images before their release. Our modifications enhance the image's retrievability, with backpropagation of the loss through a deep neural network subject to perceptual constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that activated images significantly boost retrieval and copy detection accuracy, with improvements ranging from +40% for various image collections and search databases, while maintaining photo editing detection robustness. Activated images are also comparable to standard ones in terms of storage requirements and are easily searchable using a simplified, accuracy-optimal indexing technique. The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, often exceeding hundreds, by considering the context of each entity. However, the common approach to acquire supervised training data through human annotation is costly and limits the scope for new entity types. To mitigate this issue, distilling knowledge from existing annotated data and incorporating unsupervised pre-training has gained significant attention in improving FG-NET performance. 

Current pre-training methods primarily rely on Euclidean space, ignoring the hierarchical relationships between entity types. As a result, they struggle to effectively extract knowledge from data sets featuring extensive entity type hierarchies. 

To address this limitation, FGNET-RH presents a novel framework for performing FG-NET using hyperbolic space. This approach captures hierarchical relationships between entity types by embedding the taxonomy in a hyperbolic manifold and then proposes a local aggregation strategy to combine the extracted knowledge from class neighbors. 

FGNET-RH also includes a refinement mechanism that leverages hierarchical relationships between entity types to improve its performance. This mechanism makes use of a hyperbolic-based aggregator that predicts the closest super-types for actual entity types and then aggregates the predictions of the classifier for the current entity type from its super-types. 

Experiments on six publicly accessible FG-NET data sets demonstrate that FGNET-RH outperforms the existing state-of-the-art FGNET models, even those that perform pre-training in hyperbolic space. Moreover, the proposed framework achieves comparable results with existing structured prediction methods on one data set (TDA) but surpasses their performance on the remaining data sets. 

The implementation of FGNET-RH and the associated code are publicly accessible at this link: https://github.com/ashish-91/FGNET-RH. The hyperbolic space-based source code is hosted at this link: https://github.com/ashish-91/hyperbolic_space-based_models. 

In terms of the research contributions, FGNET-RH makes the following two key contributions: 
1. It presents a novel hyperbolic space-based framework for performing FG-NET, particularly by capturing the hierarchical relationships between entity types and improving the performance of the distillation process. 
2. It also introduces a refinement mechanism that aggregates the predicted super-types of the entity types by their neighbors in the hierarchy and improves the overall FGNET-RH performance. 

FGNET-RH's source code and the associated implementation can be found at the link below: https://github.com/ashish

Achieving efficient and sustainable operation in cloud data centers largely relies on load balancing, and virtualization enables this by using virtual load balancing techniques, specifically targeting composable virtual networks. The existing approaches, such as preemptive scheduling and postpartition, aim to ensure that virtual machines receive their required network resources on time, but they have limitations. In contrast, a new virtual load balancing approach, called prepartition, prioritizes the network needs of virtual machines and schedules reservations effectively by simulating real-time network demands during the scheduling process. Since real-time network demands may vary, prepartition considers the worst-case scenario to guarantee sufficient network capacity for all virtual machines, thereby preventing overbooking. This approach ensures that virtual machines receive their reserved network resources on time, and since it involves worst-case scenarios, prepartition leads to more conservative and efficient resource usage, reducing network overbooking in data centers. Simulation results demonstrate that prepartition offers better QoS and less network overbooking compared to other virtual load balancing approaches. Furthermore, a prototype implementation allows prepartition to function in both offline and online modes, and experimental results validate its efficiency and feasibility.

In modeling systems of rival agents as games, assuming each party makes rational decisions, the probable outcomes can be identified using equilibrium concepts like the Nash equilibrium. In various real-world scenarios, factors like random events, changes in conditions, or the actions of opposing agents hinder rational decision-making. Nonetheless, it's plausible to anticipate that, in the absence of extreme circumstances, the likely outcomes will conform to equilibrium states. We introduce fixed-point networks, a proposed architecture that tackles this problem. By incorporating a fixed-point layer, this architecture enhances the model's capacity to approximate game equilibria more effectively. We demonstrate the FPNet architecture's advantages in both classification and regression tasks within the context of board games. We also compare fpnet against current methods for predicting equilibria, such as counterfactual recurrent networks and vanishing gradient recurrent networks, and demonstrate fpnet's capability to handle non-differentiable operators and large-scale games that defy efficient solutions with current methods. We validate fpnet's performance by evaluating its predictions against actual human decisions in the game of chess and Scrabble. Significant physical harm can result from cyber assaults on Industrial Control Systems. Although in-person assaults may be detected through predictive monitoring of system behaviour, this possibility could dissuade an adversary from carrying out a stealthy attack on the system. We examine the situation where a stealthy attack affects a physical system's behaviour, and the system's initial state and unknown input are unknown. We propose an in-real-time operational framework for identifying whether the system is behaving normally, has been compromised by a stealthy attack, or is experiencing malfunctioning behaviour that is not the result of an attack. The framework relies on a polytope-based characterisation of the system and incorporates predictive observations through least squares residual testing. The effectiveness of our technique is demonstrated using the example of a 1-dimensional vibration-based monitoring system on a physical scale. Our attack has a success rate of less than 0.03% when there is no malfunction and less than 0.01% when there is a known malfunction compared to the total number of possible inputs. Recently, Variation Autoencoders have emerged as a preferred choice for unsupervised learning of intricate probability distributions. Compared to traditional autoencoders, VAEs exhibit enhanced reconstructive capabilities, making more accurate approximations possible even in the presence of random noise. By utilizing a hierarchical prior distribution and integrating a regularizing loss in the objective function, VAEs function as a framework for both learning and recognizing generative models. Nevertheless, the existing approaches to accounting for noise through regularizing losses are unclear and confusing, and previous studies have only explored simple scenarios. Furthermore, the relationship between the model and data sizes in VAEs needs to be further investigated. We propose a robust and efficient variant of VAE, known as LS-VAE, by modifying the objective function to make the model more suitable for generative tasks. Additionally, we develop a comprehensive theoretical framework for analyzing the characteristics of LS-VAE, which helps in obtaining the approximate values of unknown parameters. We establish that LS-VAE is adaptable to various data sizes, and its objective function has a non-asymmetric form. We also perform an empirical evaluation of LS-VAE to verify its effectiveness in numerous applications, such as image construction and handwritten digit generation. We empirically demonstrate that LS-VAE produces a simpler and more coherent model with a lower number of trainable parameters, ultimately yielding better performance. We hope the insights obtained from this analysis will contribute to improving the performance of LS-VAE and its variants. Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty arises from class imbalance and uncertainties in labeling, issues that are particularly prevalent in datasets consisting of images of ancient Greek papyri such as AL-ALL and AL-PUB, which we also examine. However, these datasets present an additional layer of complexity due to their subjective nature - evaluating images that are often blurry, poorly lit, or obfuscated by various forms of degradation requires a considerable degree of technical expertise and specialized knowledge. To effectively address the inconsistencies in crowdsourced datasets, we suggest a novel ensemble method that incorporates both soft and hard voting mechanisms, particularly suited for class-balanced forecasting and uncertainty quantification tasks. This proposed ensemble method is capable of producing reliable results in class-imbalanced datasets, even when the network is trained on an uneven mix of easy and hard examples. Moreover, we provide insights into strategic labeling, partial relabeling, and partial reweighting techniques to effectively mitigate the influence of noisy labels. Finally, we offer a label correction method that adjusts network outputs based on Shannon's entropy and optimal classification in both normal and hard voting schemes. To formally present our contributions, we have made our code and a paper available for public access at https://github.com/afsharim/HSV-Journal-submission. As an additional step, we have also conducted thorough experiments to verify the reliability of our numerical findings by repeating them three times. Our code has been successfully tested on Ubuntu 20.06 and Python 3.8.10, with our methodology having been validated on an assortment of modern neural network architectures, including 5 different ConvNets, 5 ResNets, 5 Ensemble models, 5 recurrent models, 5 TransNets, and 5 non-linear regression models. Large data-driven companies have considered online controlled experiments (A/B Testing) a gold standard for six decades. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" to evaluate these experiments. This method, however, has limitations due to its focus on reliable estimates, which often require large sample sizes to achieve statistical significance. This results in two issues: first, the tests are difficult to plan and often take a long time to provide insights, and second, the findings may lack consistency due to varying sample sizes in different tests. To overcome these challenges, this paper proposes a new approach that aims to control the false discovery rate in large A/B testing scenarios, particularly those involving dependent datasets. This method, called "Controlled FDR," takes into account the dependence between groups to provide tighter bounds for statistical inference. By applying this approach, companies can run a smaller number of tests, plan less time in advance, and increase their ability to detect meaningful treatment effects at a given false positive rate. To validate the method, this paper uses real-world data from Google Ads. Monte Carlo simulations are also conducted to compare the performance of this approach with existing methods under different levels of dependence between groups. Finally, this paper applies the method to actual online controlled experiments to demonstrate its effectiveness and provide meaningful treatment effect detection results. The proposed method has been implemented in a GitHub repository and made available for public use. To the best knowledge of the authors, this method has been originally contributed to the field of large-scale statistical inference. To further reproduce the results, the real-world data and associated plots can be accessed. This paper outlines a new approach for detecting treatment effects while maintaining a controlled false discovery rate under dependency between groups, which may have the potential to significantly improve the field of statistical inference and online controlled experiments. To expand on this idea, a related work is described below. A similar approach had been explored in the thesis "Statistical Inference in Large-Scale A/B Testing" by the primary author, which also provides additional insights and mathematical derivations that support the method. The proposed method has been adapted from the authors' initial work on "Online Cross-Dataset Experiments with Multiple Asynchronous Traces," which introduced a method to detect patterns in large datasets by reducing the impact of dependency between groups using a sparse regularization technique. In an effort to resolve the anomalies in both the W boson and muon (g-2), we have investigated the type-X two Higgs doublet model. Our analysis focused on the type-X 2HDM's parameter space for $X$ values between $-10$ and $-0.1$ below the weak scale, considering constraints from the muon (g-2), sin$^2\theta_W$, the mass of the Z boson, electroweak fits, and dark matter relations with the Higgs portal. To determine if this model could adequately explain the observed masses of the W and Higgs bosons, we have determined the former's mass for various $X$ values and $m_H$. As an added aspect, we have also studied the type-X 2HDM's potential role in explaining both the W boson and muon (g-2) anomalies if the former's mass remains consistent with its CDF II prediction made prior to the latest data release. Our analysis showed that with sufficient fine-tuning of approximately $3\sigma$ and $5\sigma$ in accounts, we have found the type-X 2HDM parameters that could satisfy the constraints mentioned. Our study has also compared the type-X 2HDM's predictions with the latest results from direct searches for the Higgs sector. Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, it's necessary to analyze various acoustic characteristics and compare them through multiple measurement techniques. This work introduces a novel turn-level metric, referred to as the Neural Entrainment Distance (NED), developed using an unsupervised deep learning approach. NED establishes a method for identifying patterns within a dataset and uses them to create a common representation from disparate signs. By testing the measure with a selection of acoustic features, it demonstrates better performance in distinguishing between speakers compared to traditional methods. Moreover, it's proven that NED captures the essence of entrainment by correlating strongly with human assessments of the same acoustic features in a subjective study. NED's effectiveness in detecting patterns in various tasks and its potential for identifying predictive features related to entrainment make it a valuable tool for speech research. Moreover, it's shown that NED's supervised variants can be used as performance indicators for speech synthesis systems and potentially serve as a target for speech generation systems aiming to mimic natural, human-like conversations. Classifying every video frame into its respective action can be a labor-intensive task, particularly for a large collection of unlabeled videos. Therefore, we present a novel, unsupervised method to segment actions in videos without relying on labeled data. Our approach, called SSCAP, relies on a self-supervised model that captures contextual information from individual frames and their temporal relationships within a video. SSCAP utilizes frame-wise action correlations to derive a coarse segmentation of videos. To achieve this, we develop a novel loss function called CoAP that facilitates SSCAP to approximate the frame-wise action segmentation. Furthermore, we adapt Transfer Learning to establish a common action language across different videos, enabling SSCAP to identify actions within contexts. Through comprehensive testing on benchmark datasets, SSCAP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised action segmentation. Additionally, SSCAP achieves results comparable to fully supervised methods when labels are available. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by reinforcing key testing concepts through feedback. We aim to improve this aspect by introducing Testing Tutor, a platform that offers various testing pedagogies and a customizable feedback engine. An empirical study comparing the impact of traditional and conceptual feedback on two groups of sophomore students was conducted. By providing students with either code-focused or concept-based feedback using Testing Tutor, our study demonstrated that conceptual feedback led to increased code coverage, fewer unnecessary test cases, and improved programming concepts, as evidenced by a related questionnaire. While the group receiving conceptual feedback initially faced a shorter period of adaption, it ultimately provided more long-term benefits. Our study suggests that while both approaches can be useful, incorporating conceptual feedback and inquiry-based learning into testing education can lead to more efficient and long-term understanding of testing principles. By adopting this method, educators can prepare students not only to write effective test cases but also to develop a deeper understanding of testing as a skill that benefits both academic and professional pursuits. An empirical study was also conducted to compare the impact of Testing Tutor's concept-based and code-based feedback mechanisms. The study indicated that students prefer the code-based feedback option due to its greater similarity to the feedback they would receive in professional settings, as provided by tools like SonarQube. However, our testing and qualitative analysis showed that the concept-based approach was superior in various aspects. The study produced five findings, which can be summarized as the preferences of students for the code-based feedback, the benefits and limitations of the concept-based and code-based approaches respectively, the factors that contribute to these preferences, and the potential improvements that could be incorporated into the code-based feedback option. These findings are such that they can be applied across various educational platforms. The code and demonstration video for this empirical study can be accessed at the specified link. Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, researchers have been turning to independent approaches incorporating remote sensing data and microcensus statistics. These developments led to the creation of novel systems such as cuckoo and xor filters, which effectively addressed this issue. Moreover, adaptive solutions have recently been introduced, enabling the avoidance of potential errors in data queries for specific elements. This research aims to introduce a new type of static filter that eliminates incorrect positive results for negative data sets, thus further enhancing the efficiency of data retrieval. We have developed a new family of probabilistic filters called the singleton filter, specifically designed to effectively handle queries of the form 'does not contain?' without producing any incorrect positive results. We compare the efficiency of the singleton filter to that of compressed static filters while utilizing significantly less memory. We introduce an improved variant of the singleton filter, called the singleton prefix filter, for handling queries of the form 'contains?' regarding elements of a limited size, achieved through prefix compression. Furthermore, our results have demonstrated that an optimized variant of the singleton prefix filter can provide memory savings of up to 50 times when compared to compressed static filters of the same level of precision. We have conducted extensive experiments to compare its performance to that of other filters. Our contribution has the potential to significantly impact systems requiring a low false positive rate and can be applied to various data retrieval applications. We have also outlined a possible extension of this idea, specifically a low false negative rate filter, and have suggested additional areas of improvement for future research. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions involving spin transfer. In situations where final molecule formation is constrained, this leads to the creation of two molecules and one unpaired atom, which can be viewed as a coherent version of three-body recombination in systems with one spin unit. In the dark-state condition, we determined the cross-section for producing one molecule and a spin doublet atom to be directly proportional to the square of the light's detuning, which diverges as the light frequency moves further from the resonance with the spin doublet. Furthermore, we have outlined a protocol to produce pairs of spin-singlet and spin-doublet molecules using spatially inhomogeneous light and an optical trap with a minimum point that converges as it moves through the resonance. As a result, this method may offer a means to study three-body recombination in systems with one spin unit by producing coherent superposition of atom and molecule states. Finally, we have discussed how to produce the coherent superposition of clock states necessary for the highly accurate Geonium oscillator, which could be developed using a more sophisticated version of this light-trap design. In the dark-state condition, we found the amplitude of the clock superposition to be directly proportional to the square of the light's detuning, which may offer a more straightforward path to the highly coherent superposition required for geonium oscillator construction. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets has significant implications for various scientific and technical disciplines. The development of quantum computing has the potential to create a revolutionary quantum machine learning framework. Unlike traditional AI methods, quantum algorithms can potentially solve complex problems and provide better outcomes by leveraging quantum physics principles such as the famous Shor algorithm and D-Wave devices. Despite these promises, there are two main challenges to implementing quantum machine learning systems. First, most existing approaches rely on classical data preparation, which is prone to data preparation biases and hinders the development of universal quantum learning machines. Second, the lack of universal quantum learning machines is due in part to the difficulty of reconfiguring quantum circuits, which are time-consuming to adjust as the number of qubits increases. To address these issues, we have developed a new learning algorithm that can perform unsupervised learning on quantum circuits with mixed-mode operations. The algorithm can preprocess data and create a custom quantum circuit to match the circuit's configuration, thus enabling the conversion of data from one circuit structure to another. We have also implemented a supervised learning prototype that uses a superconducting quantum processor and has achieved a 94.0% classification accuracy on a dataset of binary images. This achievement demonstrates the potential for reconfigurable quantum processors to excel in machine learning applications. The ability to perform both unsupervised and supervised learning on a single reconfigurable quantum processor represents a major step towards the development of a universal quantum learning machine. The resulting approach has been successfully tested with real-world data and is expected to contribute significantly to the creation of a universal quantum learning machine. A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's given pitch values far from its average pitch value.  In other words, it has limited pitch controllability.  We suggest two new algorithms to improve the limited pitch controllability of FastPitch.  First, we came up with a way to change pitch while preserving the model's timbre for small changes in pitch.  This allowed us to create more pitch variations by applying the timbre-preserved pitch changes multiple times.  Second, we used FastPitch to create a male speaker voice from a short amount of data, and we changed its pitch to mimic a female speaker's pitch.  This allowed us to train the model using the speaker's natural pitch values, which improved its ability to change pitch.  Now FastPitch can create speech with more natural pitch using a fixed model, and the quality of the speech created by FastPitch in the original and modified versions is the same.  We also compared our algorithm to another method of pitch augmentation and found that our algorithm changed the model's pitch more successfully.  This work is going to be a part of a larger system to change text pitch without changing the text's meaning.  This system will be released as open-source. This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object persistence principles. A crucial element of our approach is recognizing how to connect features from different frames that pertain to the same object. This problem is known as aligning long-range dependencies in objects across multiple frames. To resolve this issue, we've developed a model called Hopper, which incorporates a long-range self-attention mechanism. By allowing the model to hop features from one frame to another, this mechanism enables the retrieval of dependencies from distant frames and facilitates the establishment of object-based connections across different time frames. Our experimental results show that the Hopper model excels in its ability to perform a single-hop, multiply-hop, and long-range attention-based operation. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that the singly-hop model is more efficient and just as effective as the single-hop model. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate that the Hopper model outperforms the cross-attention model in various cases, while also revealing that the singly-hop model shows weaker performance in multiply-hop scenarios where attention is not applied. With these observations in mind, we propose a combination of our models, which yields superior results when applied to multiple steps in a process. When subjected to testing on the TIR-SGBD dataset, our model demonstrates an impressive mAP performance of 63.19%, which significantly surpasses the existing state-of-the-art performance of 58.35%. In this study, we revisit the basic features of two Bayesian hierarchical regression models, considering a hierarchical model for both the dependent and independent variables, and then expand on these models by incorporating additional covariates into the distributions for the group-level means and the precision parameters. The models and their associated inference methods are presented in detail, and their performance is compared to traditional methods of estimation and testing using a Monte Carlo simulation. These models are then applied to a real-world data set from a study on glass fragmentation under impact. The findings suggest that including additional covariates in the prior distributions for the group-level means and the precision parameters can affect inference capabilities, such that the inclusion of these covaiates can sometimes broaden or narrow the confidence intervals for the regression coefficients and group-level means, and potentially shift the means of the model residuals, either making them more consistent with normal distribution or altering their shape. The proposed models manage to explain the residual patterns in the data set, providing better accuracy and fit compared to other models such as linear regression, the random effects model, the mixed effects model, the penalised regression model and the Bayesian lattice model. understand how their formation is affected when planets develop in tandem. Our
study uses long-term computer simulations of planetary growth from a shared gas
disk, and the results reveal a link between the planets' relative sizes and the
formation of gaps in the disk. However, when both planets form simultaneously,
their masses converge to a narrow range over a relatively short period of time.
Delaying one planet's development slightly increases their size disparity but
ultimately yields a similar mass ratio. To replicate observed exoplanet mass
variations, models suggest planets form and grow at different times and then
either disperse quickly from the gas disk or have gas supply interrupted early. 
Although once common, two-planet systems are now less frequently detected, and
our models imply that such systems contribute to the diversity of planetary sizes. 
When one planet finishes growing before the other, disk gaps form and affect
the smaller planet's ability to accumulate gas, and the larger planet's mass is
not affected until the smaller planet clears its own orbit, resulting in a
bimodal mass distribution for second planets in systems like $\epsilon$ Telus A.

evolve over a long period, and the resulting systems mainly consist of single giant
planets or have the smaller planet significantly more massive than the larger
planet. These results imply possible explanations for the scarcity of two-planet
systems but also vary based on the stage of planetary development and gas remaining
in the disk at its conclusion. 
Lastly, the models imply that two-planet systems often retain their structural
characteristics for an extended period, and the resulting systems typically have
the smaller planet roughly half as massive as the larger planet.

achieve a similar mass to the larger planet until the gas in the disk diminishes,
and the larger planet has cleared its orbit.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in relevance and importance, affecting the quality of the cluster. To overcome this limitation, our method modifies the traditional fuzzy k-means objective function using two distinct entropy terms. The first term optimizes cluster compactness by maximizing inter-cluster separation and minimizing within-cluster variance. The second term dynamically weights features according to their unique contributions, promoting better data partitioning. The effectiveness of our approach is evaluated through multiple datasets and comparisons with established state-of-the-art clustering methods. Compared to these methods, our algorithm yields higher average accuracy, higher connectivity of clusters, and better feature stability. Furthermore, our results indicate that our algorithm performs exceptionally well in clustering high-dimensional data. Additionally, our method generates compact and well-defined clusters, suitable for further analysis and interpretation beyond clustering. The proposed algorithm has potential applications in areas such as data visualization and downstream machine learning tasks. The implementation and results of our approach can be found on GitHub. The article also includes a thorough analysis and discussion of the method's components, inspired by the principles of the Rao entropy. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite extensive research over two decades. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution to this long-standing problem by introducing an innovative algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE model parameters based on empirical observations. Our new algorithm is founded on the em algorithm, a method that iteratively updates parameters by temporarily fixing some, but not all, model components. This innovative approach is backed by theoretical analysis showing that both E-step and M-step updates are asymptotically accurate under certain conditions, a level of proof that has yet to be achieved in the MoE literature. Our study also includes the implementation and evaluation of this new algorithm on a variety of real-world datasets, resulting in substantial improvements in convergence and predictive accuracy compared to existing methods. Our results indicate that the new algorithm is capable of learning complex Gaussian mixture models, even when the number of components exceeds the amount of data available, a challenge that previously proved elusive to existing methods. Additionally, the paper extends this concept to address the related problem of unsupervised kernel selection for kernel machines and solves a long-standing open issue in this area. Our algorithm is further accompanied by a complementary method for approximating the em algorithm at finite length, which helps to mitigate issues of instability in the algorithm's later stages. Our study includes the implementation and evaluation of this additional method on real-world datasets as well. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower neural networks with predictive capabilities through pre-trained models. This paper presents findings that challenge two widely accepted assumptions about DTL: (1) generally comparable classification abilities of neural networks even in the absence of supervision, and (2) the claim that knowledge is accumulated through deep networks absorbing data from various sources. By conducting thorough examinations, we came across two counterintuitive observations: (a) there exists a simple data augmentation technique that greatly enhances the classification performance of DTL, and (b) using a more complex network structure can actually impair the models' ability to recognize patterns in target domains. These discoveries lead us to suggest that instead of attributing the success of DTL to complex network architectures, we should consider the importance of understanding how DTL works as a form of data augmentation. This is an area that remains largely underexplored. Our proposed method aims to improve DTL by applying a unified objective that combines both classification and adversarial processes in the feature space, resulting in the evolution of DTL as a sophisticated form of data augmentation. This is achieved by removing unnecessary features from the feature map, effectively enabling the models to focus on target domain characteristics during the training process. Consequently, the models' ability to recognize patterns in target domains is greatly enhanced, and there is no need for pre-training. This is to say that both source and target domains have an equal opportunity to shape the feature map. Our proposed method consistently surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in DTL, as evidenced by the experimental results presented in this paper. Moreover, the results show that the proposed method is more robust than expected, even when there is a significant gap in the data distribution between the source and target domains. This is to say that the proposed method is capable of handling more complex scenarios. Therefore, the proposed method is highly recommended for use in future DTL projects. discrete nonlinear interference points and find that this distance can be employed to estimate 
the effective memory length of the communication channel. By expressing this distance in terms 
of the secondary user's detection power, we establish a bound on this distance, thereby 
limiting the effective memory length and the error in our discrete-time model. Our analysis 
demonstrates that as the signal-to-noise ratio decreases, the error in our discrete-time model 
increases, while an increase in this value causes the model's accuracy to approach the memory 
length of the channel, which is a continuous-time property. Ultimately, we apply our findings to 
quantify the accuracy of our discrete-time model for a specific communication channel 
characterized by exponential decay. We show that our discrete-time model can achieve 
accuracies of up to two orders of magnitude higher than continuous-time models, while the 
discrete sampling rate required for this accuracy depends on the secondary user's detection power 
and the ratio of the channel's bandwidth to the sampling rate.  Therefore, our discrete-time

This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for facilitating communication between humans and a swarm of robots. Our solution involves merging a compact hand gesture recognition model with the advanced \emph{ros2} system to enable a swarm of robots to execute complex actions in response to distinct hand signals. Our experiment, utilizing a series of hand gestures that instruct different swarm behaviors, was successfully implemented with three Turtlebot3 robots. This enabled these robots to automatically adjust their distances and evade collisions with obstacles in various simulated environments as well as in a physical testing setup. Our research paves the way for future research to extend this interaction system to incorporate more sophisticated swarm controls. Additionally, future developments could also involve integrating other modalities of human input, such as vocal instructions. The study aims to assess different neural network architectures for classifying white and red blood cells, features that hold significant importance in diagnosing various medical conditions. Given the potential of deep learning models to achieve high accuracy in medical feature classification, the authors investigate and compare the feasibility of three neural network architectures - CNN, RNN, and CAPS - in classifying distinct blood cells. Our findings reveal that CAPs achieved the best accuracy overall, with RNNs providing more accurate classifications for red blood cells, and CNNs offering relatively lower predictions. For future work, the authors suggest exploring integrated CAP models, combining the strengths of CNN and RNN components. As the model currently suffers from low precision and complexity issues, the authors propose adapting strategies like dropout and Bayesian training to mitigate these problems. Additionally, the authors recommend investigating the feasibility of the model in diagnosing rare blood conditions using red blood cell classifications. Our final model was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation, resulting in macro-averaged F1 scores of 0.713 for red cells, 0.700 for white cells, and 0.675 for cell classification overall. The code used in this research has been made publicly available via GitHub at https://github.com/apapavlas/ blood-cell-classification. As the study demonstrates that deep learning models can achieve high accuracy in classifying blood cell features, the authors recommend combining such models with expert analysis to enhance the diagnosis of rare medical conditions. Current ITN techniques mostly rely on machine learning models using contextual speech-to-text data, although this approach is limited by the availability of such data. A new method is proposed to tackle this problem by utilizing written language data alone, relying on a neural ITN model that can learn to remove speech characteristics. We demonstrate that this method can effectively translate ASR output into written text across various domains without requiring contextual speech data. Furthermore, we show that data augmentation techniques can significantly enhance the performance of this approach by eliminating the need for speech data in most cases. We also investigate how domain flexibility affects ITN and find that the written language used in a domain greatly influences its ITN requirements. We therefore establish standard ITN tasks for three domains: news, conversations, and novels. We evaluate our proposed method and compare it to other powerful ITN models, revealing the efficiency and domain flexibility of this approach that can be easily scaled up by using data augmentation techniques to tackle various ITN tasks. We also open-source our method for public use. Comprehensive experiments and analysis are performed to validate our method. Moreover, we test its real-world application in Amazon's Alexa service and demonstrate its practical efficiency. Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In an effort to enhance classification and layer understanding, we've developed a novel network that combines multiple neural tangent kernels - one for each layer - as opposed to earlier work focusing on a single kernel to represent the entire network. We validate the effectiveness of this model on two datasets, revealing that it successfully reveals the intricate relationships between the network's layers and its predictive abilities. Additionally, we use a new framework to calculate the expressive capacity of neural tangent kernels, based on our prior research. Notably, our findings on the MNIST and CIFAR datasets show that the channel basis offers better representation quality compared to the Fourier basis. Ultimately, we use the NTK model to achieve state-of-the-art results on the icospheres dataset, while also exploring new avenues for kernel designs, such as learning them based on the dataset's structure, rather than the network's architecture. This research offers insights into the relationships between neural networks, kernel models, and the expressiveness of neural tangent kernels, potentially leading to new kernel designs that can help achieve state-of-the-art results in representation, classification, and layer understanding tasks. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information metric on a simplified level for model selection. This approach is represented by two specific models based on the original problem: the Poisson Group Lasso model and the Bernoulli Group Lasso model. The former applies to data with multiple categories, and the latter to binary data. We conduct a series of simulations and use a real-world dataset from a medical study on subjects with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to assess the performance of our method in comparison to other existing approaches. Additionally, we provide a justifications for the consistency of our models through theoretical proofs. Ultimately, the results validate the effectiveness of our method in achieving a sparse solution, consistent with the findings of other studies, and providing a a meaningful interpretation of the results. Many portable devices such as smartphones and tablets naturally assume a vertical orientation. To take advantage of this inherent orientation, we have developed a simplified approach to stitching panoramic images by utilizing the direction of gravity as a reference point. By considering the gravitational axis as a fixed entity, we have formulated the stitching process as a continuous path problem while minimizing the total rotation required. Our proposed method does not require identifying distinct landmarks or applying complex optimization techniques. Instead, we have demonstrated that the stitching path can be effectively determined by analyzing the radial directions of feature points and adjusting for minor discrepancies. Our experimental results show that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to traditional approaches while being more efficient, especially in cases where the features are weak. Additionally, we have created a JavaScript implementation of the proposed method that can be easily embedded in mobile browsers for real-time applications. Our tests have confirmed that the implemented approach runs swiftly on modern web browsers. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we have employed a standardized metric that combines both category and grade level to assess the similarity between pairs of images. Our results indicate that the proposed method achieves an average similarity score of 0.76 ± 0.01, which signifies that the images generated by the proposed method are 76% similar in content to the original images, as determined by the human eye. Our experimental findings also show that the proposed method is robust when applied to images captured using either smartphones or tablets. Our analysis of the performance of the proposed method reveals that the features extracted from images captured using tablets are slightly easier to identify and localize. This research introduces SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. It utilizes PyTorch for the classical components, allowing for the creation of multiple quantum models that can be optimized with back-propagation. We demonstrate SQUID's capabilities by showcasing its implementation in a standard binary classification task from the widely-used MNIST dataset. Notably, we discuss how the choice of output affects the scalability of quantum models when utilizing gradient-based optimization. We compare the performance of these different quantum models against a traditional SVM classifier and a fully classical CNN. Additionally, we explore the application of different initialization techniques and training methods to enhance the model's resistance to overfitting. We further examine the impact of limited quantum resources by evaluating our models' robustness to changes in qubit number and circuit depth. Our results highlight the importance of designing algorithms that can exploit the advantages of quantum computing while minimizing its limitations.
